questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with fever and weight loss. He gives a history of blood in the stools and vomiting 2 weeks ago. On examination, there is right hypochondriac tenderness and hepatomegaly. Abdominal CT a lesion in the right lobe of the liver with ragged edges, multiple septations, and heterogenous densities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amoebic liver abscess

Features of fever, hepatomegaly, and hypochondriac tenderness are suggestive of a liver abscess. A liver abscess in a patient with a history of blood in the stools and vomiting points to a diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.

Amoebic liver abscess is more common in males in the age group of 20 - 40 years with a history of travel to endemic areas. Ingestion of Entamoeba histolytica cysts causes diarrhea initially. Following this, the trophozoites reach the liver through the portal venous system and cause an amebic liver abscess. 80% of the cases involve the right lobe. The clinical features of amoebic liver abscess are right upper quadrant pain, tenderness, fever, hepatomegaly, and diarrhea.

Enzyme immunoassays detecting the presence of antibodies against the parasite have high sensitivity and specificity. Ultrasonography and CT scans can visualize the liver abscess without a peripheral rim of enhancement.

The mainstay of treatment for amebic abscesses is metronidazole, which is curative in more than 90% of patients. Luminal agents such as diloxanide furoate can be administered to treat the carrier state. Aspiration of abscess is recommended in case of a high risk of rupture. Pigtail catheter drainage is done in patients not responding to intravenous metronidazole in the first 48–72 hours to improve antibiotic penetration.

Option A: Pyogenic liver abscess is usually seen after 50 years of age and is not associated with a history of travel or diarrhea. Jaundice, bacteremia, and positive blood cultures are common in pyogenic liver abscesses compared to amoebic liver abscesses. Serology testing for Entamoeba is negative. A characteristic rim enhancement is noted in the case of a pyogenic abscess on a CECT abdomen and can differentiate it from an amoebic liver abscess.

Option B: Hydatid cyst a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species of flatworms. Primary hydatid cysts most commonly occur in the liver. Most patients are asymptomatic but when symptomatic, the patient presents with hepatomegaly, pain, and obstructive jaundice. The rupture of a hydatic cyst can result in fever, pruritus, or anaphylaxis. Imaging findings are cystic lesion with multiple daughter cysts within, detachment of the endocyst membrane (water-lily sign on USG shown below), and areas of calcification.

Option D: Hemangiomas are more common in women and are usually asymptomatic. Larger hemangiomas may present with vague upper abdominal symptoms. On contrast-enhanced CT scan, hemangiomas show asymmetrical, nodular peripheral enhancement that is isodense, with large vessels and progressive centripetal enhancement.
questions.learning: Amoebic liver abscess Features of fever, hepatomegaly, and hypochondriac tenderness are suggestive of a liver abscess. A liver abscess in a patient with a history of blood in the stools and vomiting points to a diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An affected male does not have affected children but an affected female always has affected children. Type of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mitochondrial

In mitochondrial inheritance, if the mother is affected and the father is normal, then all their children (both male and female) will be affected. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother will not be affected.

The mitochondrial inheritance pattern is as shown in the image below:

The unique feature of mitochondrial inheritance is maternal inheritance, as the disease is transmitted through the affected mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria.

The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa has very few mitochondria if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum.

Therefore, affected mother transmits the disease to all the offsprings (both male and female), and only the daughters of the affected mother, will further transmit the disease.

Characteristic features of mitochondrial inheritance:

• The mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes required for oxidative phosphorylation. Therefore, organs that are most dependent on the oxidative phosphorylation are the ones most affected in diseases due to mutations in mtDNA. These organs include central nervous system, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, liver, and kidneys.
• There are several thousands of copies of mtDNA in each mitochondria, of which only a few copies are affected in case of mutation. Therefore, a diseased individual possesses copies of both wild type mtDNA and mutant mtDNA in each mitochondria  This phenomenon is called heteroplasmy.
• The disease manifests if a minimum number of copies of mutant mtDNA are present in the mitochondria that can lead to oxidative dysfunction, called the threshold effect. In most cases, this threshold effect is reached in the organs as mentioned above.
• Also, during a cell division, the wild and mutant copies of the mtDNA are unequally distributed among the daughter cells. As a result, the expression of the disease varies even among different cells of an organ.
questions.learning: Mitochondrial — In mitochondrial inheritance, if the mother is affected and the father is normal, then all their children (both male and female) will be affected.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young athlete was diagnosed to have HOCM and has a harsh ejection systolic murmur. Which of the following maneuvers would most likely increase the intensity of the murmur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Valsalva maneuver

HOCM is characterized by:

• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
• Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT)

This obstruction varies depending on ventricular volume.

Correct answer is B because Valsalva maneuver decreases venous return and left ventricular preload, which worsens left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in HOCM and increases murmur intensity.

Isometric handgrip and squatting increase preload/afterload and reduce obstruction, decreasing murmur intensity. Leaning forward is classically used to accentuate aortic regurgitation murmur.
questions.learning: Valsalva maneuver HOCM is characterized by: • Asymmetric septal hypertrophy • Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) This obstruction varies depending on ventricular volume.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the organism from the given staining technique.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nocardia asteroids

The organism shown above is the Nocardia species. The above image shows acid-fast staining, where the organisms are shown appear as acid-fast (stained with fuschia) and branching rods or filaments. They are aerobes found particularly in the soil and are found to produce lung infections in the immunocompromised.

Options A, B: Mycobacteria species are acid-fast but do not have branching filaments.

Option C: Actinomyces species is gram-positive but not acid-fast.
questions.learning: Nocardia asteroids — The organism shown above is the Nocardia species. The above image shows acid-fast staining, where the organisms are shown appear as acid-fast (stained with fuschia) and branching rods or filaments.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: How long should a child be isolated after being diagnosed with bacterial meningitis to prevent further transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Till 24 hours after starting antibiotics

Isolation of the child is recommended until 24 hrs after the initiation of effective therapy after being diagnosed with acute bacterial meningitis to prevent further transmission.

Droplet precautions are recommended for patients with Neisseria meningitides and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis until they have received 24 hours of effective therapy. Patients should be in private rooms, and hospital personnel should wear a face mask when they are within 3 feet (1 meter) of the patient.

The child with meningitis shows nonspecific symptoms like fever, anorexia, poor feeding, headache, myalgia, hypotension, petechia, purpura, or a rash. Meningial irritation is indicated by nuchal rigidity, back pain, and Kernig, and Brudzinski signs (usually not seen in infants). Seizures and altered mental status may be present.

The recommended empirical antibiotic regimen in a suspected case of meningitis outside the neonatal period is vancomycin combined with a third-generation cephalosporin. Patients allergic to penicillin or cephalosporin can be treated with meropenem, fluoroquinolones, or chloramphenicol.

Chemoprophylaxis with rifampicin/ceftriaxone/ciprofloxacin is recommended for all close contacts with meningococcal meningitis regardless of age or immunization status. Rifampicin prophylaxis should be given to all household contacts of patients with invasive disease caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, if an immunocompromised child of any age resides in the household or close family member younger than 48 months has not been fully immunized.
questions.learning: Till 24 hours after starting antibiotics Isolation of the child is recommended until 24 hrs after the initiation of effective therapy after being diagnosed with acute bacterial meningitis to prevent further transmission.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended method for the initial screening of cervical cancer among women at the primary health care level?
options: Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution
questions.explanation: In resource-limited settings like a Primary Health Center (PHC) in India, the most practical and effective screening method is "Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA)". This involves applying a 3% to 5% acetic acid solution to the cervix; pre-cancerous or cancerous lesions turn white ("aceto-white") and can be easily seen by a trained health worker. Colposcopy (Option B) and Cervical biopsy (Option C) are "confirmatory" tests performed at higher centers (District hospitals or Medical colleges) once a screening test is positive. High vaginal biopsy (Option D) is not a standard screening tool. VIA is preferred over the Pap smear at the primary level because it provides "immediate results," allows for the "see-and-treat" approach, and does not require complex laboratory infrastructure. Screening is recommended for women aged 30-65 to reduce mortality from this highly preventable cancer
questions.learning: In resource-limited settings like a Primary Health Center (PHC) in India, the most practical and effective screening method is "Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA)".

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With which variety of asbestos, Mesothelioma has been shown to have a strong association?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crocidolite

Mesothelioma is a highly aggressive malignancy arising from the pleura or peritoneum and is strongly associated with occupational asbestos exposure. Among the different types of asbestos, crocidolite (blue asbestos) has the strongest association with malignant mesothelioma because of its thin, straight fibers, which penetrate deep into the lungs and pleura.

High-Yield Pearls

• Crocidolite (blue asbestos) has the strongest association with mesothelioma. ⭐
• Chrysotile (white asbestos) is the most commonly used form of asbestos but is less strongly associated with mesothelioma than crocidolite. ⭐
• Amosite (brown asbestos) also increases the risk of mesothelioma but less than crocidolite.
• Anthophyllite is the least commonly used and least strongly associated with asbestos-related malignancy.
questions.learning: Crocidolite Mesothelioma is a highly aggressive malignancy arising from the pleura or peritoneum and is strongly associated with occupational asbestos exposure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a history of chronic ear infection presents with fever, headache, vomiting, irritability, and confusion. His CT brain is shown in the image below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal lobe abscess

The clinical vignette depicting features of CNS infection (fever, headache, vomiting, and confusion) in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess.

Temporal lobe abscess is an intracranial complication that can arise from chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).

Brain abscess typically progresses through four stages. The first stage is the stage of invasion (initial encephalitis), which often goes unnoticed. Symptoms such as headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and drowsiness may be present.

The second stage is the stage of localization (latent abscess), during which a capsule forms around the abscess, effectively localizing the pus.

The third stage is the stage of enlargement (manifest abscess). The abscess enlarges, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and the development of edema surrounding the abscess. As a result, symptoms worsen.

The final stage is the stage of termination (rupture of abscess). At this point, the abscess expands and eventually ruptures into the ventricle or subarachnoid space, which can result in potentially fatal meningitis.

Signs of raised ICP may include headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, papilledema, and coma.

Characteristic findings associated with temporal lobe abscess include nominal aphasia, homonymous hemianopia, seizures, contralateral motor paralysis, pupillary changes, and oculomotor palsy.

The preferred diagnostic imaging modality for temporal lobe abscess is a CT scan of the brain. This imaging study reveals a ring-enhancing lesion indicative of a brain abscess.

Medical treatment involves initiating intravenous antibiotics, typically metronidazole. Raised ICP can be addressed using dexamethasone or mannitol.

Surgical intervention is the definitive management and involves drainage of the abscess followed by radical mastoidectomy to address the underlying CSOM.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebellar abscess is a form of brain abscess and is usually associated with an otogenic source of infection. It can occur as a direct extension through Trautmann's triangle or via retrograde thrombophlebitis.

An MRI image showing cerebellar abscess is given below:

Option C: Subdural abscess refers to the focal collection of purulent material between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

An MRI image showing subdural abscess is given below:

Option D: Meningitis is the inflammation of the leptomeninges which includes the arachnoid mater and pia mater. It can be due to an infectious or noninfectious etiology. It presents with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, and signs of meningeal irritation. Ring enhancing lesion on neuroimaging is not a feature of meningitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD with a history of URTI and poor academic performance. He breathes through his mouth and has a high-arched palate. What type of hearing loss can be expected in this child? URTI- Upper respiratory tract infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conductive hearing loss

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing and a high-arched palate points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by conductive hearing loss.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterised by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of the tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably rhinolalia clausa (hyponasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, or tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild earaches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* A thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterised by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high-arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss, and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Primary auditory canal cholesteatoma is characterised by normal hearing.

Option C: Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic condition characterised by sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary abnormalities (such as two different coloured eyes or early graying of hair), and dystopia canthorum (widely spaced eyes).

Option D: A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve
questions.learning: Conductive hearing loss — The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing and a high-arched palate points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by conductive hearing loss.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following inhalational agents has the blood-gas partition coefficient similar to Nitrous oxide?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Desflurane

Desflurane is the inhalational anesthetic agent with the blood-gas partition coefficient similar to Nitrous oxide.

Among the commonly used inhalational anesthetics, desflurane is the least fat-soluble which leads to a faster recovery. Desflurane is also minimally metabolized by the liver, thereby reducing hepatotoxicity.

Inhalational agent
Blood-gas partition coefficient

Halothane
2.5

Isoflurane
1.4

Sevoflurane
0.65

Desflurane
0.45

Nitrous oxide
0.4

Blood-gas partition co-efficient determines the solubility of the anesthetic agent in the blood. The higher the blood-gas partition coefficient, the higher will be the solubility of the anesthetic agent. This leads to its greater uptake by pulmonary circulation. The higher the uptake of the anesthetic agent, the higher the difference between the inspired and alveolar concentrations, which leads to a slower rate of induction and recovery. Desflurane has a very low blood:gas partition coefficient (0.42). Thus, the alveolar and blood concentrations rapidly rise to the level of inspired concentration, providing rapid induction of anesthesia and rapid recovery.

Other options:

Option A- Halothane is a high fat-soluble agent and can result in halothane hepatitis due to increased metabolism in obese individuals. Hence it is avoided.

Option C- Sevoflurane has a relatively higher fat solubility compared to desflurane.

Option D- Isoflurane has a higher fat-gas partition co-efficient resulting in increased recovery time from anesthesia.
questions.learning: Desflurane Desflurane is the inhalational anesthetic agent with the blood-gas partition coefficient similar to Nitrous oxide. Among the commonly used inhalational anesthetics, desflurane is the least fat-soluble which leads to a faster recovery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 72-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain. She describes excruciating pain, but abdominal examination reveals only mild tenderness, with pain out of proportion to physical findings. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Serum lactate elevation is always present in the early stage. 2. Atrial fibrillation is a risk factor. 3. CT angiography is the investigation of choice. 4. Pain out of proportion to physical findings is a classic feature.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3 and 4

Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is a surgical emergency resulting from sudden interruption of intestinal blood flow. The classic presentation is severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, particularly in patients with atrial fibrillation, which predisposes to superior mesenteric artery embolism. CT angiography (CTA) is the investigation of choice for early diagnosis.

• 2. Atrial fibrillation is a risk factor ✓: AF is the most common cause of arterial embolic acute mesenteric ischemia.
• 3. CT angiography is the investigation of choice ✓: It rapidly identifies arterial occlusion, bowel ischemia, and guides management.
• 4. Pain out of proportion to physical findings is a classic feature ✓: A hallmark of early acute mesenteric ischemia.

Why is statement 1 incorrect?

• 1. Serum lactate elevation is always present in the early stage ✗: False. Serum lactate may be normal early in the disease and typically rises only after significant bowel ischemia or infarction. Therefore, a normal lactate does not exclude AMI.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is a surgical emergency resulting from sudden interruption of intestinal blood flow. The classic presentation is severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, particularly in patients…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with fever, weight loss, and a painless swelling in the jaw region. His CBC shows anemia with lymphocytosis, and biopsy of the swelling suggests a malignant process. Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a rapidly growing, painless jaw swelling in a child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt's lymphoma. The diagnostic histological hallmark, as seen in the provided image, is the "starry sky appearance". This pattern is created by large, pale-staining tingible-body macrophages (the "stars") that have phagocytosed apoptotic debris, scattered against a dense background of dark, rapidly dividing malignant B-cells (the "sky"). Hodgkin’s disease (Option A) would show Reed-Sternberg cells. Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (Option B) usually presents with more generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly rather than an isolated jaw mass. Chloroma (Option C) is an extramedullary mass of leukemic cells associated with AML. Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and a characteristic translocation involving the MYC gene. It is one of the fastest-growing human tumors but is often highly responsive to intensive chemotherapy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a rapidly growing, painless jaw swelling in a child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt's lymphoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is tachypneic and hypotensive. On examination, there is decreased breath sound on the left side with dullness to percussion. A chest tube is inserted, and 1700 mL of blood is immediately drained. Over the next 2 hours, an additional 250 mL/hour of blood continues to drain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue observation with chest tube drainage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency thoracotomy

Massive hemothorax is defined by:

• Immediate drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood after chest tube insertion, or
• Persistent bleeding of more than 200 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours

This patient has:

• Initial output = 1700 mL
• Ongoing bleeding = 250 mL/hour

Both criteria are met, indicating ongoing major intrathoracic bleeding requiring surgical intervention.

Emergency thoracotomy is indicated to:

• Identify and control the source of bleeding
• Prevent hemorrhagic shock and death

Other Options:

Option A. Observation is inappropriate due to massive and ongoing blood loss

Option B. Second chest tube does not address the source of bleeding

Option D. Tranexamic acid may be adjunctive but not definitive management

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about non-invasive prenatal testing?
options: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum
It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome. It is not a diagnostic test.

It is a novel genetic test that uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum for screening of chromosomal anomalies.

DNA from the fetus is found circulating in the maternal blood in two forms - either inside the intact fetal cells or as cell-free DNA from the breakdown of placental fetal cells. In NIPT, the cell-free chromosome fragments are measured and the quantitative differences from normal fetuses are noted.

NIPT can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation and is recommended after the routine first-trimester ultrasound assessment in high-risk pregnancies or if either 1st or 2nd-trimester screening becomes positive. Its disadvantage is that it is very expensive and it can be used for screening of only a few chromosomal anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21 and it doesn't analyse the entire karyotype.
questions.learning: It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what vertebral level does the part marked in the image lie in a normal anatomical position?
options: Disc space between L4 and L5
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tip of coccyx

In the right pelvic bone given above the marked structure is the ischial spine which lies approximately at the level of the fifth sacral vertebrae in a normal anatomical position. As the tip of the coccyx is the closest option relating to the spine , it can be the most appropriate answer.

The ischial spine is a bony prominence found on the ischium, one of the three bones that make up the hip bone. The ischial spine forms a part of the plane of least pelvic dimensions or narrow pelvic plane which comprises of :

• lower border of the symphysis pubis
• the tip of ischial spines
• fifth sacral vertebra

The interspinous distance is the distance between the tip of two ischial spines. ( Bispinous diameter = 10.5 cm or 4.5" )

The important events occurring at the narrowest plane in the pelvis :

• It corresponds roughly to the origin of levator ani muscles.
• The internal rotation of the fetal head occurs during labour at this plane.
• It marks the beginning of the forward curve of the pelvic axis
• This level of ischial spines indicates station ‘O’
• When the fetal head station is at ‘O’, the head is considered to be engaged.
• Deep transverse arrest occurs at this plane.
• The ischial spine can serve as a landmark in pudendal anaesthesia, as the pudendal nerve lies close to the ischial spine

The image given below highlights the interspinous distance seen through the pelvic inlet.
questions.learning: Tip of coccyx — In the right pelvic bone given above the marked structure is the ischial spine which lies approximately at the level of the fifth sacral vertebrae in a normal anatomical position.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall onto an outstretched hand. The following cast was applied to the patient. What fracture did the patient suffer from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass-holding position is known as the scaphoid cast/glass-holding cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion, as if a glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray does not show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Extra-articular fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar or ventral displacement (Image below).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What type of joint exists between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
questions.explanation: The joint between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of a growing long bone is the epiphyseal plate (growth plate), which is a type of synchondrosis. This is a primary cartilaginous joint where the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage. These joints are typically temporary and allow for longitudinal bone growth. A symphysis (Option A) is a secondary cartilaginous joint where bones are joined by fibrocartilage, such as the pubic symphysis or intervertebral discs. A synostosis (Option C) occurs when a joint completely ossifies and becomes bone, which is what happens to the epiphyseal plate once growth is complete. A syndesmosis (Option D) is a fibrous joint where bones are joined by an interosseous ligament, like the inferior tibiofibular joint. Understanding the nature of the epiphyseal plate is critical in pediatric orthopedics, particularly when managing Salter-Harris fractures, which involve injuries through this cartilage layer and can potentially lead to stunted or asymmetric limb growth if not treated correctly
questions.learning: The joint between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of a growing long bone is the epiphyseal plate (growth plate), which is a type of synchondrosis. This is a primary cartilaginous joint where the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with a pterygium that has been steadily progressing towards the pupillary area. What is the best means of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Excision with conjunctival autograft

The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft.

A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it comprises elastotic degenerative changes in vascularised subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts:

* cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge)

* head

* body

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism.

Treatment:

* A pterygium is best left alone unless:

* It is progressing towards the pupillary area

* Causes excessive astigmatism

* Restricts ocular motility

* Causes disfigurement.

* Excision: A simple pterygium excision often leads to a high chance of recurrence. Measures to prevent recurrence are:

* Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.

* Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis.

* Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures.

* Amniotic membrane graft

* Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep.

Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also), of which conjunctival autografting has fewer recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure that reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning, and necrosis.

Note:

A combination of conjunctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.
questions.learning: Excision with conjunctival autograft — The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn baby presented with a difficulty in breathing. Auscultation of the chest revealed gurgling sounds and heart sounds shifted to the right. The chest radiograph confirmed a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Which among the following is the most common location for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left posterolateral

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with the features given in the clinical vignette occurs most commonly in a left posterolateral defect.

Bochdalek hernia is the most common congenital diaphragmatic hernia which occurs on the left posterolateral side due to a defect in the pleuroperitoneal membrane. The abdominal contents in the thorax compress the developing lungs causing pulmonary hypoplasia which manifests as respiratory distress in most infants. Chest X-ray shows an indistinct diaphragm with radiolucent para cardiac shadow and absent bowel loops in the abdomen. Opacities can be seen in the thorax if solid organs or omentum also herniate. Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Given below is an X-ray showing Bochdalek's hernia

Other options:

Option A- Sliding and rolling hernias occur via the oesophagal opening(hiatal hernia). Sliding hernia (more common) occurs when the gastroesophageal junction(GEJ) and a part of the stomach slide up into the thorax via the opening. A rolling hernia occurs when the GEJ stays below the diaphragm, but the stomach goes up, lying parallel to the oesophagus in the thorax. Hiatal hernias occur in adults.

Option C- The space between the sternum and costal cartilage is called the space of Larry or space of Morgagni. A defect in this space causes Morgagni hernia, which is the second most common hernia in children. It occurs on the right anteromedial aspect and is often less symptomatic.

The following is an X-ray showing Morgagni's Hernia :

Option D- A defect in the central tendon causes a central congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about diphtheria toxin? a. It inhibits EF-2 b. It is an A-B type exotoxin c. It primarily affects the myocardium and nerves d. Toxin is produced only by strains carrying a plasmid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a, b and c

Diphtheria toxin is a phage-encoded A-B exotoxin produced by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2) by ADP-ribosylation, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis and causing cell death. The toxin primarily affects the myocardium and peripheral nerves, leading to myocarditis and neuropathy, the major life-threatening complications of diphtheria.

Why is B correct?

• a. Inhibits EF-2 ✓: Blocks protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of EF-2.
• b. It is an A-B type exotoxin ✓: The A (active) subunit inhibits protein synthesis, while the B (binding) subunit mediates entry into host cells.
• c. It primarily affects the myocardium and nerves ✓: Responsible for myocarditis, arrhythmias, and peripheral neuritis.
• d. Toxin is produced only by strains carrying a plasmid ✗: The tox gene is carried by a lysogenic β-corynephage, not a plasmid.
questions.learning: a, b and c Diphtheria toxin is a phage-encoded A-B exotoxin produced by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2) by ADP-ribosylation, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis and causing cell death.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the jugular venous pressure (JVP), the "a" wave is related to:
options: Tricuspid valve bulging into the right atria
questions.explanation: The "a" wave in the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform corresponds directly to right atrial contraction (systole). This contraction causes a transient increase in atrial pressure, pushing blood into the ventricle and halting venous inflow. Tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium (Option B) corresponds to the "c" wave, which occurs during isovolumetric ventricular contraction. Right atrial relaxation (Option C) occurs after the "a" wave and contributes to the "x" descent. Right atrial filling (Option D) corresponds to the "v" wave, which represents venous return filling the atrium while the tricuspid valve is still closed. The JVP is a critical clinical tool for assessing right heart function, with the "a" wave specifically reflecting the effectiveness of atrial systole just before the first heart sound
questions.learning: The "a" wave in the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform corresponds directly to right atrial contraction (systole). This contraction causes a transient increase in atrial pressure, pushing blood into the ventricle and halting venous inflow.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of renal tubules reabsorbs maximum water in the presence of ADH?
questions.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) acts mainly on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing their permeability to water by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the tubular membrane. This allows maximum water reabsorption under the influence of ADH. Although a large amount of water (~65%) is reabsorbed in the PCT, this process is ADH-independent (obligatory reabsorption). The question specifically asks for water reabsorption in the presence of ADH, making the collecting duct the correct answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) PCT: Reabsorbs maximum water overall, but not regulated by ADH (B) DCT: ADH has some effect, but less significant than in collecting duct (C) Loop of Henle: Descending limb is water-permeable but not under ADH control Thus, ADH-dependent maximal water reabsorption occurs in the collecting duct
questions.learning: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) acts mainly on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing their permeability to water by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the tubular membrane.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following new drugs has been approved for the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Edaravone

Edaravone was approved by the FDA for the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

It has free radical scavenging properties that may reduce oxidative stress. The exact mechanism of action is unknown. It is to be administered as an IV infusion with an initial treatment cycle of daily dosing for 14 days, followed by a 14-day drug-free period. Subsequent treatment cycles consist of dosing on 10 of 14 days, followed by a 14 day drug-free period.

The major adverse effect of edaravone is hypersensitivity because the infusion contains sodium bisulfite. Other adverse effects include bruising, gait disorder, and headache.

Tafinlar (dabrafenib) and Mekinist (trametinib), are both indicated as monotherapy in BRAF V600E/K (BRAF V600E mutation-positive) melanoma. They are approved for combined administration, for the treatment of anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) that cannot be removed by surgery or that has spread to other parts of the body (metastatic).

Piracetam is a nootropic agent (a drug that enhances cognitive function) that is used off-label to enhance memory. It is also used to treat myoclonus.
questions.learning: Edaravone Edaravone was approved by the FDA for the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It has free radical scavenging properties that may reduce oxidative stress.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. On assessment, he opens his eyes only in response to painful stimuli, exhibits abnormal flexion to pain, and produces disoriented verbal responses. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is calculated by summing the scores for Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). For this patient: Eye opening (E): Opens to pain = 2 points. Verbal response (V): Disoriented/Confused = 4 points. Motor response (M): Abnormal flexion (withdrawal) to pain = 3 points. Total GCS = 2 + 4 + 3 = 9. Options A (11), B (12), and C (10) are incorrect based on these specific clinical findings. A GCS of 9–12 indicates moderate brain injury. If the patient had been oriented (V=5) or obeyed commands (M=6), the score would be higher. Conversely, extension to pain (M=2) or incomprehensible sounds (V=2) would yield a lower score. This objective assessment is vital for neurological monitoring and determining the need for advanced airway management
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is calculated by summing the scores for Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). For this patient: Eye opening (E): Opens to pain = 2 points.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the emergency management of asthma does not act by bronchodilation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hydrocortisone

Hydrocortisone does not act by bronchodilation while all other drugs mentioned act by bronchodilation.

Mechanism of action of Corticosteroids in an acute asthma attack:

* Increases responsiveness to Beta-2 agonists

* Decreases mucous secretion

* Decreases the inflammatory cell response.

Steroids increase the transcription of beta 2 receptor genes and hence increase responsiveness to beta-2 agonists. Beta-2 agonists, on the other hand, increase the effect of steroids by enhancing the action of glucocorticoid receptors.

Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma

Bronchodilators

* Beta-2 sympathomimetics: Salmeterol, Formoterol

* Methylxanthines: Theophylline, Aminophylline

* Anticholinergics: Ipratropium bromide, Tiotropium bromide

Anti-inflammatory

* Corticosteroids (Inhalational): Beclomethasone, Budesonide, Fluticasone

* Corticosteroids (Systemic): Prednisolone, Hydrocortisone

* Mast cell stabilizers: Sodium cromoglycate, Ketotifen

* Leukotriene antagonists: Montelukast, Zafirlukast

* anti-IgE - Omalizumab

* anti-IL5 - Mepolizumab, Reslizumab(IL-5 antagonist), Benralizumab(IL-5 receptor antagonist)

* anti-IL4 receptor - Dupilumab

Treatment guidelines for different types of asthma are given below:

Step 1 (intermittent)
As needed low dose ICS + Formoterol

Step 2 (mild persistent)
Daily low-dose ICS

Step 3 (moderate persistent)
Daily low dose ICS + LABA

Step 4 (severe persistent)
Medium dose ICS + LABA +/- add-on therapy

Step 5
High dose ICS + LABA + oral steroids +/- add-on therapy

LABA - Long-acting Beta 2 Agonists, ICS - Inhaled corticosteroids
Add-on therapy includes long-acting anticholinergics, leukotriene antagonists, mast cell stabilizers, methylxanthines, and antibodies.

Other options:

Option A: β2 selective agonists like salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol, etc, cause relaxation of the tracheal and bronchial smooth muscles by β2 receptor agonist action.

Option B: Ipratropium bromide acts by antagonizing muscarinic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, thereby causing bronchodilation.

Option C: Theophyllines increase the effects of steroids by activating the enzyme histone deacetylase, which is the target for steroids as well.

Highest mineralocorticoid activity is seen with aldosterone.

Highest mineralocorticoid activity in a drug that is clinically used is seen with fludrocortisone (aldosterone cannot be used clinically).

Least mineralocorticoid activity is seen with methylprednisolone.

Highest glucocorticoid activity is seen with dexamethasone and betamethasone.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension, tachycardia, and early renal involvement is started on an angiotensin receptor blocker (telmisartan). By which mechanism does this drug most effectively help in reducing heart rate and blood pressure?
options: By increasing sodium excretion via loop diuretics
questions.explanation: Telmisartan is an Angiotensin II Receptor Blocker (ARB) that acts as a selective competitive antagonist at AT1 receptors. Its primary mechanism for lowering blood pressure is through potent vasodilation, which results in a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance. By reducing systemic pressure, ARBs can also lead to a secondary reduction in reflex sympathetic activation, which helps improve tachycardia. ARBs do not directly decrease cardiac output (Option B), as they lack significant negative inotropic properties. They are not loop diuretics (Option C); these belong to an entirely different drug class. Option D (beta-1 receptor blockade) is the mechanism of beta-blockers like propranolol, not ARBs. Telmisartan is particularly useful in patients with renal involvement because it reduces intraglomerular pressure, providing a renoprotective effect

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man is referred from the infertility clinic to the surgical OPD after palpation reveals a “bag of worms” sensation along with dilated veins in the scrotum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The pathognomonic physical finding of a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum is diagnostic of a Varicocele. This condition involves the abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins in the pampiniform plexus. It is most commonly found on the left side due to the anatomical drainage of the left spermatic vein into the renal vein. Varicoceles are a leading cause of correctable male infertility because the blood pooling increases scrotal temperature, which impairs spermatogenesis. Testicular torsion (Option C) is an acute surgical emergency presenting with sudden, severe pain. Hydrocele (Option A) presents as a painless, transilluminant fluid collection. Epididymo-orchitis (Option D) is an inflammatory condition characterized by acute pain, swelling, and often fever. Given the specific context of the infertility clinic referral and the characteristic "bag of worms" palpation, varicocele is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves surgical ligation or embolization of the dilated veins
questions.learning: The pathognomonic physical finding of a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum is diagnostic of a Varicocele. This condition involves the abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins in the pampiniform plexus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome requires the presence of which of the following clinical features? 1. Menstrual irregularity 2. Clinical or biochemical androgen excess 3. Multiple cysts in the ovaries 4. BMI <18.5 kg/m² Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is diagnosed using the Revised Rotterdam criteria (2003), which require any two of the following three features after excluding other causes of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction:

1. Ovulatory dysfunction – Oligo-ovulation or anovulation, presenting as menstrual irregularity (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea).
2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism – Hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia, or elevated serum androgen levels.
3. Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasonography.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Menstrual irregularity: Correct. Menstrual irregularity reflects chronic anovulation and is one of the diagnostic criteria.
• Statement 2. Clinical or biochemical androgen excess: Correct. Clinical or biochemical androgen excess is a core diagnostic feature.
• Statement 3. Multiple cysts in the ovaries: Correct. Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound is one of the Rotterdam criteria.
• Statement 4. BMI <18.5 kg/m²: Incorrect. BMI <18.5 kg/m² is not a diagnostic criterion. Although many women with PCOS are overweight or obese, lean PCOS is also well recognized.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised A 1.5-year-old child is brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, body temperature of less than 37 degrees, cough, and cold. On examination, the respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Administer IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

This child with a respiratory rate of 46 breaths/min has tachypnea/fast breathing without any danger signs has pneumonia according to IMNCI guidelines. The next best step of management is to administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home.

The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

* Cough and cold, no pneumonia - requires home remedy

* Pneumonia - with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

* Severe pneumonia - pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

Tachypnea or Fast breathing is defined based on the age and respiratory rate:

Age of child
Rate

<2 months
60 breaths/min

2-12 months
50 breaths/min

1-5 years
40 breaths/min

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatitis B

Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against Hepatitis B.

These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste.

Yearly health check-ups should be done, and a booster dose should be given if needed.

Post-exposure prophylaxis for HBV:

When the Hepatitis B status of the source patient is unknown: HCW is managed as if the source patient were HBsAg-positive.

When the source patient is HBV-positive:

* HCW whose response is unknown after one round of HBV vaccination - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and should simultaneously reinitiate the course of HBV immunization with three doses of hepatitis B vaccine.

* HCW is a non-responder after two rounds of HBV vaccination - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and a second dose of HBIG, 1 month after the first dose.

* Healthcare worker (HCW) is immunized and a responder (anti-HBs antibodies >10 mIU/ml) - They are protected. No need for hepatitis B immunoglobulin after a potential or confirmed exposure to hepatitis B.

* HCW is incompletely vaccinated/unvaccinated - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and should simultaneously start/reinitiate the course of HBV immunization with three doses of hepatitis B vaccine.

Follow-up: After the three-dose vaccination series is completed, antibodies to the surface antigen is checked 1–2 months later. If the titres are <10 mIU/ml a second three-dose vaccine series is started or the HCW is checked for HBsAg positivity.

Some other vaccines that are given to healthcare workers include:

* Tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap) vaccine

* Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine

* Influenza vaccine

* Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine

* Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine
questions.learning: Hepatitis B Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against Hepatitis B. These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling in the right parotid region. FNAC confirms a malignant parotid tumor. The surgeon wants to assess the first group of lymph nodes involved in metastasis. The lymph nodes involved will be:
options: Preauricular and superficial parotid lymph nodes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preauricular and superficial parotid lymph nodes

The parotid gland has an extensive intraparotid lymphatic network. Malignant tumors of the parotid gland first metastasize to the intraparotid (superficial parotid) and preauricular lymph nodes, before spreading to the upper deep cervical lymph nodes (Level II).

The patient has a malignant parotid tumor. The first-echelon (sentinel) lymph nodes are:

• Preauricular lymph nodes
• Superficial (intraparotid) lymph nodes

Why not the other options?

• A. Submental lymph nodes: Drain the lower lip, chin, floor of mouth, and tip of the tongue, not the parotid gland.
• B. Deep cervical lymph nodes: Involved later after spread from intraparotid nodes.
• D. Submandibular lymph nodes: Drain the submandibular gland, oral cavity, cheeks, and anterior tongue, not the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is incorrectly matched with its corresponding enzyme?
options: Vitamin B9 (Folic acid): FIGLU excretion/ Histidine load test
questions.explanation: The pairing of Vitamin C with serum methylmalonate (MMA) levels is incorrect. Serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) is a specific and sensitive metabolic marker used to diagnose Vitamin B12 deficiency, not Vitamin C. In the absence of B12, methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be converted to succinyl-CoA, leading to elevated MMA. All other pairings are correct clinical markers: RBC transketolase activity is used to assess Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) status (Option A). RBC glutathione reductase activity is the standard test for Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) status (Option B). FIGLU (formiminoglutamic acid) excretion after a histidine load is a classic functional test for Vitamin B9 (Folic acid) deficiency (Option C). Vitamin C status is typically measured through plasma or leukocyte ascorbic acid levels. Therefore, Option D is the definitive "incorrect" pairing according to standard biochemical diagnostic protocols
questions.learning: The pairing of Vitamin C with serum methylmalonate (MMA) levels is incorrect. Serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) is a specific and sensitive metabolic marker used to diagnose Vitamin B12 deficiency, not Vitamin C.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual periods, acne, and excessive hair growth. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum insulin and testosterone levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of irregular periods (ovulatory dysfunction), acne, and excessive hair growth (hirsutism), combined with laboratory findings of elevated testosterone and insulin, is pathognomonic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a complex endocrine disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance. Endometriosis (Option B) typically presents with severe pelvic pain and infertility but not hyperandrogenic features. While certain virilizing ovarian tumors (Option C) can cause high testosterone, they usually present with rapid onset of symptoms rather than a chronic history. Hypothyroidism (Option D) can cause menstrual irregularities but is not associated with hirsutism or acne. Management of PCOS involves lifestyle modifications to address insulin resistance, along with hormonal contraceptives or anti-androgens to manage the skin and cycle issues. It is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility in reproductive-age women
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of irregular periods (ovulatory dysfunction), acne, and excessive hair growth (hirsutism), combined with laboratory findings of elevated testosterone and insulin, is pathognomonic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

| Type | Exudative

| Cells | Lymphocyte predominant

| ADA | ↑↑ (>40 IU/L highly suggestive)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the action of the muscle at the hip, which is attached to the marked area in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extension and lateral rotation

The image shows the posterior surface of the femur, and the structure marked is gluteal tuberosity, to which the gluteus maximus muscle is attached. It causes extension and lateral rotation at the hip joint.

The femur can be divided into:

• The proximal femur - Consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface.
• The shaft of the femur - Consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line
• The distal femur - Consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.

Gluteus maximus muscle:

Origin:

• Posterior aspect of the dorsal ilium, posterior to the posterior gluteal line
• Posterior superior iliac spine
• Posterior aspect of sacrum and coccyx
• Sacrotuberous ligament.

Insertion - It is inserted mainly in fascia lata at the iliotibial band and also into the gluteal tuberosity on the posterior femoral surface.

Action:

• Major extensor of the hip joint
• Lateral rotation of the hip joint
• Active in powerful abduction of the thigh

Arterial Supply - Inferior and superior gluteal arteries and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery.

Nerve Supply- Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1 and S2).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a child with a unilateral undescended testis, a diagnostic laparoscopy is performed which showed the blind-ending testicular vessels on the right side. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No further exploration

In non-palpable testis cases, laparoscopically encountering blind-ending vas deferens and testicular vessels prior to entering the internal ring is sufficient to diagnose a vanishing testis. In such cases, no further exploration is required.

Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The descent of the testes can arrest anywhere, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

• Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.
• Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role.

Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:

1. Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization
2. Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis
3. Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells

It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma).
questions.learning: No further exploration — In non-palpable testis cases, laparoscopically encountering blind-ending vas deferens and testicular vessels prior to entering the internal ring is sufficient to diagnose a vanishing testis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presents to you with complaints of feeling light-headedness and dizziness when she lies on her back and feels relieved if she lies on her side or when walks. What is the most likely reason behind this?
options: Excessive venous pooling at the feet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVC compression

This condition is known as Supine Hypotensive Syndrome. In late pregnancy, the enlarged uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies on her back.

Gravid uterus compresses IVC

↓

Reduced venous return to heart

↓

Decreased cardiac output

↓

Maternal hypotension

↓

Dizziness and light-headedness

Common features include:

| Symptom | Reason

| ------- | ------

| Dizziness | Reduced cerebral perfusion

| Nausea | Hypotension

| Pallor | Decreased cardiac output

| Tachycardia | Compensatory response

It may also reduce uteroplacental blood flow.

Best management:

• Left lateral position

This shifts the uterus away from the vena cava.

Supine position → IVC compression

Left lateral position → venous return restored

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with complaints of a painful lid swelling. Physical examination reveals a swollen and painful lid with a pus point on the lid margin. Which of the following glands is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zeis gland

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hordeolum externum, or stye, which is a staphylococcal infection of the Zeis glands.

Hordeolum externum or stye is a staphylococcal infection of the Zeis gland or Moll gland. It presents as a collection of pus usually pointing at the base of a single cilium. The entire lid may be edematous. Treatment is with antibiotics and a warm compress. The abscess may also be drained by pulling out the affected cilia. Incision and drainage may also be done.

Other options:

Option A: Acute dacryoadenitis, which is the inflammation of the lacrimal gland, is typically associated with painful swelling of the lateral part of the upper lid, leading to an S-shaped swelling. Painful proptosis may also be observed.

Option B: Hordeolum internum is the suppurative inflammation of the Meibomian gland and may occur as a primary infection or secondary to infected chalazion. There is a tender swelling with a pus point facing toward the tarsal conjunctiva. The image below shows an internal hordeolum.

Option D: The glands of Krause and Wolfring are accessory conjunctival glands.

Pearl PF1388: Layers of the Tear Film

Lipid layer

* Outermost layer

* Secreted by the meibomian, Zeis glands

* Prevents evaporation of tears

Aqueous layer

* Middle layer

* Secreted by the lacrimal and accessory lacrimal glands

* Provides lubrication

Mucin layer

* Innermost layer

* Secreted by the goblet cells of the conjunctiva

* Help in spreading the tear film over the ocular surface

The maximum density of the goblet cells is seen on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of migraine? I. It is associated with dilatation of extracranial vessels II. Common migraine is seen without aura III. Aura is most often visual
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Migraine is a primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe, usually unilateral, throbbing headache, often associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. It is believed to result from activation of the trigeminovascular system, leading to release of vasoactive neuropeptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which causes vasodilatation of extracranial vessels and neurogenic inflammation.

All three statements are correct:

• I. It is associated with dilatation of extracranial vessels
• II. Common migraine is seen without aura (Migraine without aura accounts for 80–85% of cases)
• III. Aura is most often visual (e.g., scintillating scotoma, flashing lights, zig-zag lines.)
questions.learning: I, II and III Migraine is a primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe, usually unilateral, throbbing headache, often associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which type of hanging does weight of the head, arms and chest act as a constricting force?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial

The weight of the head, arms, and chest acts as a constricting force in partial hanging.

Types of hanging:

* Complete hanging: Here the weight of the entire body acts as a constricting force.

* Partial hanging: The bodies are partially suspended, the weight of the head (5-6 kgs), arms, and chest act as a constricting force.

* Typical hanging: In this, the ligature runs from the midline above the thyroid cartilage symmetrically upward on both sides of the neck to the occipital region. A knot of the ligature is on the backside of the neck.

* Atypical hanging: The knot of the ligature is anywhere other than on the backside of the neck. Usually, the knot is near the mastoid process or angle of mandible. Occasionally, it may be under the chin.

In India, the knot is tied under the angle of the right jaw. On drawing the bolt, the person drops to the length of the rope. The sudden stoppage of the moving body associated with the position of the knot causes the head to be jerked violently.

Judicial hanging:

* The face of the person is covered with a dark mask, stand on a platform above trapdoors,which open downwards when the blot is drawn.

* Rope is looped around the neck and the person is allowed to drop for 5-7 meters according to weight, age and build.

* Sudden stop causes fracture dislocation at the level C-2, C-3 or C-3/C-4 vertebra and rupture between pons and medulla (hangman fracture).

* Death is instantaneous, but the heartbeat may continue for 15-20 minutes and spasmodic muscle jerking may occur for a considerable time.

* Asphyxial signs are not seen in correctly performed judicial hangings.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Cellular junctions present in a cardiac muscle are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zonula occludens

Zonula occludens is the other name for the tight junction. It is absent in a cardiac muscle.

Cardiac muscle cells are connected by Fascia adherens (a structural analog of zonula adherens), Gap junctions and Macula adherens.

Cardiac muscle fibers are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel to one another. The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another are called intercalated disks. At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gap junction which provides low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber to another permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium.
questions.learning: Zonula occludens Zonula occludens is the other name for the tight junction. Cardiac muscle cells are connected by Fascia adherens (a structural analog of zonula adherens), Gap junctions and Macula adherens.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea. Investigations revealed that his HbA1C is 10%. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease. Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

The treatment of malignant otitis external would include control of diabetes, ear toileting to remove the discharge, debris or granulation tissue, antibiotic therapy against Pseudomonas with fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, beta-lactam antibiotics with/without aminoglycosides.

If the patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea indicates malignant otitis externa. It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What proportion of a country’s Gross National Product (GNP) is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) to be allocated toward healthcare expenditure?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) has historically and globally recommended that a nation should allocate at least 5% of its Gross National Product (GNP) for expenditure on the healthcare sector to ensure adequate provision of essential services. This target is considered the minimum investment required to achieve significant improvements in public health indicators and progress toward Universal Health Coverage. Options A (2.0%), B (2.5%), and C (3.5%) represent lower expenditure levels often seen in many developing nations, including India, which has set an intermediate national goal of reaching 2.5% of GDP by 2025. Adequate healthcare financing is critical for strengthening primary health infrastructure, ensuring the availability of essential medicines, and reducing the catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure that often pushes families into poverty. National health accounts track this spending to monitor the government's commitment to the health and well-being of its citizens. Achieving the 5% GNP target is a key barometer of a country's health system performance
questions.learning: The World Health Organization (WHO) has historically and globally recommended that a nation should allocate at least 5% of its Gross National Product (GNP) for expenditure on the healthcare sector to ensure adequate provision of essential services.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with painless loss of vision. The ocular findings are shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis and management for this patient?
options: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL

The given clinical scenario and the above image are suggestive of an immature senile cataract and the appropriate treatment is phacoemulsification with posterior intraocular lens implantation.

An immature senile cataract is characterized by partial opacification of the lens. The cuneiform and cupuliform patterns of opacification are seen and the lens appears greyish-white. Iris shadow is visible. Slit-lamp examination shows areas of the normal and cataractous cortex.

The treatment of choice for immature senile cataracts is treated by extracapsular cataract extraction by phacoemulsification and foldable posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation.

Other options:

Option A: Zonular cataract is a developmental type of cataract in which opacification occupies a discrete zone in the lens. It is the most common type of congenital cataract presenting with visual impairment. Lensectomy is the treatment of choice for congenital cataracts.

Option B: Rosette cataract presents after close globe injuries (blunt trauma) resulting in damage to the lens fibers and capsule resulting in hydration of lens fibers by aqueous humor. This results in opacification of the posterior subcapsular cortex along the posterior sutures. It presents as a flower-shaped opacification. Iridodialysis occurs due to dehiscence of the iris from the ciliary body at its root. The pupil becomes D-shaped. Surgery is recommended in case of visual impairment.

Option C: Sunflower cataract is seen in Wilson disease due to the deposition of cuprous oxide in the anterior lens capsule and subcapsular cortex in a stellate pattern. D-penicillamine is an effective treatment modality.
questions.learning: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL The given clinical scenario and the above image are suggestive of an immature senile cataract and the appropriate treatment is phacoemulsification with posterior intraocular lens implantation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. During an autopsy, apparent bleeding was seen on the surface of his brain. Which type of hemorrhage would not be washed away under direct running water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Subarachnoid haemorrhage will persist when washed under running water during an autopsy.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding in the space between the brain and the arachnoid membrane which is the subarachnoid space. During an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage is not easily washed away by running water. This is because it is located in this deep layer, which can trap the blood within the brain's sulci and gyri.

While doing the autopsy, there is typically some fresh blood present. However, it cannot be washed off because the blood is situated beneath the very thin and transparent arachnoid layer.

This makes the blood from a SAH less likely to be displaced compared to haemorrhages located in other regions, such as epidural or subdural spaces. Thus, despite running water during an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage often remains in place, making it detectable even after washing.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate presents with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (serum bilirubin = 28 mg/dL) requiring exchange transfusion. Genetic testing confirms absence of UGT1A1 enzyme activity. Which of the following correctly describes the urine and stool findings in this condition?
options: Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen absent, Stool stercobilinogen absent
Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen decreased, Stool stercobilinogen pale/decreased
Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen normal/slightly decreased, Stool stercobilinogen normal/slightly decreased
Urine bilirubin present, Urine urobilinogen increased, Stool stercobilinogen normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen decreased, Stool stercobilinogen pale/decreased

| Parameter | Finding | Reason

| --------- | ------- | ------

| Urine bilirubin | ❌ Absent | Only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in urine. CN has unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia → none reaches urine

| Urine urobilinogen | ⬇️ Decreased | Unconjugated bilirubin cannot enter bile → less reaches gut → less urobilinogen formed → less absorbed → less excreted in urine

| Stool stercobilinogen | ⬇️ Decreased/Pale stools | Less bilirubin reaching gut → less converted to stercobilinogen → pale stools
