questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 18-day-old baby presents with altered sensorium, and neck rigidity with vesicular lesions on the anterior abdomen and the forearm. The mother revealed a history of treatment for painful genital ulcers a year ago and the baby was born through vaginal delivery. CSF examination reveals multinucleate giant cells. Which of the following is the most likely involved organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HSV - 2

The given clinical scenario of an 18-day-old child presenting with altered sensorium, neck rigidity, and vesicular lesions on the anterior abdomen and the forearm with the mother giving a history of painful genital ulcers, is suggestive of neonatal herpes due to herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2. CSF examination with multinucleate giant cells with CNS manifestations indicates neonatal meningitis to the DNA virus.

Painful genital ulcers are commonly seen in genital herpes and chancroid due to Hemophilus ducreyi ((ducreyi makes you cry).

Herpes infection can be caused by HSV-1 and HSV-2 viruses. HSV-1 causes orofacial lesions, i.e. herpes labialis, while HSV-2 mainly causes genital herpes which is characterised by vesiculo ulcerative lesions of the penis of the male or of the cervix, vulva, vagina, and perineum of the female.

The typical herpes lesions are thin-walled, umbilicated vesicles, the roof of which breaks down, leaving tiny superficial ulcers which heal without scarring. The most common site of cutaneous lesions is in the face, cheeks, chin, around the mouth and forehead. A cesarean section is performed in a case of active genital herpes at the time of labour in order to prevent neonatal herpes infection.

One of the following three disease patterns can be seen in infants infected during delivery or in the postpartum period: (1) disease limited to the skin, eyes, or mouth; (2) encephalitis with or without skin, eye, and mouth disease; or (3) disseminated infection affecting several organs, such as the brain, lungs, liver, heart, and adrenal glands.

Infants suffering from encephalitis usually exhibit clinical symptoms that point to bacterial meningitis at 8- 17 days of life. These symptoms include seizures, poor feeding, lethargy, neck stiffness, irritability, and positive Kernig's sign. When left untreated, HSV encephalitis results in 50% of infant deaths and severe neurologic sequelae in the majority of survivors.

Acyclovir at a high dose of 60 mg/kg/day, administered intravenously every eight hours, should be the first line of treatment for any infant with a confirmed or suspected neonatal HSV infection.

Other options:

Coxsackie virus, Enterovirus and VZV are not attributed to painful genital ulcers and hence ruled out.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with fever and a rash spreading from the face, behind cheeks, and buccal mucosa to other body parts. On examination, Koplik's spot is present. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Measles

The likely diagnosis is measles based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of Koplik spots.

Koplik spots are discrete red lesions with central bluish-white spots seen on the buccal mucosa at the level of premolars.

The measles virus has an incubation period of 8-12 days, after which the prodrome phase begins with mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. This follows the appearance of maculopapular rash after 4th day of fever, which begins at the face and spreads to the torso and extremities. Lymphadenopathy may be present. Treatment is supportive. The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media.

The image below shows Koplik spots.

Other options:

Option B: Rubella presents with low-grade fever, centrifugal macular rash, and prominent lymphadenopathy (suboccipital, postauricular, and anterior cervical lymph nodes). Forchheimer spots (tiny rose-colored lesions on the soft palate) may be present.

The image below shows Forchheimer spots.

Option C: Varicella presents with fever, malaise, and anorexia, followed by a pruritic maculopapular rash, which forms vesicles with a characteristic "cropping" distribution (simultaneous presence of lesions in various stages of evolution).

Option D: Mumps presents with fever, headache, parotitis, and ipsilateral auricular pain. A morbilliform rash may occur.

questions.text: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a severe traumatic brain injury. On examination, painful stimulation elicits bilateral upper limb flexion at the elbows and wrists, with bilateral lower limb extension. This posturing pattern is most consistent with a lesion at which of the following levels, and reflects overactivity of which tract(s)?
options: Between the red nucleus and vestibular nuclei; vestibulospinal tract only
Above the red nucleus; rubrospinal and vestibulospinal tracts
Below the vestibular nuclei; reticulospinal tract only
At the level of the red nucleus; corticospinal tract only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Above the red nucleus; rubrospinal and vestibulospinal tracts

• Upper limb flexion with lower limb extension is decorticate (flexor) posturing, resulting from a lesion above the red nucleus (often involving the cerebral cortex), with overactivity of the rubrospinal and vestibulospinal tracts.
• A lesion between the red and vestibular nuclei (brainstem) instead produces decerebrate (extensor) posturing — extension of both upper and lower limbs, driven by the vestibulospinal tract alone, and carries a worse prognosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: You are an intern and want to determine the quantity of IV fluids needed for a patient. How much amount of transient loss/insensible loss per day would you account for in your calculations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 500-600 ml

500-600 ml of transient loss/insensible loss per day would have to be accounted for in the calculation.

Although water is lost through sweating especially in hot climates or during physical exertion, we tend to lose water at rest as well. Physiologically, water evaporates from the skin and lungs at a rate of about 600 to 700 ml/day. This is known as insensible water loss.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors is least likely to be involved in the development of beriberi?
questions.explanation: Beriberi is caused by a severe deficiency of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). A Vegan diet (Option B) is least likely to cause this deficiency because thiamine is widely available in many plant-based foods, including whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts. In contrast, the other options are significant risk factors. Chronic alcohol intake (Option D) is a leading cause of deficiency due to impaired absorption and poor diet. Bariatric surgery (Option C) leads to severe malabsorption and is a well-recognized trigger for acute thiamine deficiency. Chronic use of diuretics (Option A), particularly loop diuretics, increases the renal excretion of thiamine, potentially leading to depletion in patients with heart failure. Beriberi can manifest in "dry" (neurological) or "wet" (cardiovascular) forms. While vegans must be careful about Vitamin B12, they typically have adequate thiamine intake, making it an improbable cause for beriberi compared to clinical malabsorption or metabolic depletion scenarios

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 41-year-old dairy worker presents with intermittent fever, night sweats, fatigue, joint pains, and lower backache for the past 3 weeks. He admits to drinking unpasteurised milk from the dairy where he works on a regular basis. On examination, he has mild hepatosplenomegaly and tenderness over his lumbar spine. Blood cultures reveal a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Doxycycline + Rifampicin

The given clinical scenario of a 41-year-old dairy worker with intermittent fever, fatigue, joint pains, and lower backache, with frequent consumption of unpasteurised milk, is suggestive of brucellosis, which is treated with doxycycline and rifampicin.

Brucella is a gram-negative, obligate aerobic coccobacillus that causes brucellosis (undulant fever), a zoonotic febrile illness. Humans typically acquire it through occupational or domestic exposure to infected animals (like sheep, goats, and cattle) or their unpasteurised products.

Monocytes and macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system are the primary target cells for brucellosis. Brucellae are intracellular pathogens with a particular affinity for mononuclear phagocytic cells (macrophages and monocytes) found in the reticuloendothelial system (lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow). These bacteria proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system, which accounts for its resistance to simple antimicrobial therapy.

The milk ring test (MRT) is positive for Brucella. It is used for the detection of infected animals on dairy farms. In the milk ring test, whole milk is mixed with stained Brucella antigen and incubated at 70°C for 40–50 minutes

* Positive test: Antibodies agglutinate the antigen, forming a blue ring at the cream layer.

* Negative test: No ring forms; the milk remains uniformly blue.

Brucellosis can be acute or chronic. Acute brucellosis presents with muscular and articular pains, asthmatic attacks, nocturnal drenching sweats, exhaustion, anorexia, constipation, nervous irritability, and chills. Chronic brucellosis presents with sweating and joint pain with minimal or no pyrexia, and the illness lasts for years.

Rifampicin interrupts RNA synthesis by binding to a subunit of mycobacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Apart from being used to treat leprosy, it is used in the management of tuberculosis, brucellosis, and prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis. Hepatitis is a major adverse effect. Other side effects include pruritus with rash, redness and watering of eyes, flu-like symptoms, and abdominal cramps. Urine and secretions may become orange-red.

Doxycycline binds to the 30S ribosome and inhibits attachment of aminoacyl tRNA to a site of the ribosome. Photosensitivity, gastrointestinal irritation, mottling of teeth, and suppression of bone growth in children are common adverse effects of tetracycline. Doxycycline is used for prophylaxis of leptospirosis infection following exposure to contaminated water in agricultural workers following floods and natural disasters. Doxycycline is primarily eliminated through the gastrointestinal tract, making it safe for use in renal impairment, as it does not require dose adjustment in renal failure. This antibiotic avoids accumulation in patients with decreased kidney function, reducing the risk of nephrotoxicity or adverse effects related to renal impairment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A public health worker is going out into the community once every 15 days for collection of blood smears for malaria surveillance. What type of surveillance is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Active

Active case detection is done every fortnight by examination of blood smears by house visits and it is a type of active surveillance.

Malaria surveillance system:

Active case detection: Blood smears are collected by the Multipurpose Workers/Auxiliary nurse midwife on house visits every fortnight.

Passive case detection: Detection of fever cases that report to ASHAs or peripheral health volunteers.

Surveillance: There are factors which determine occurrence and distribution of diseases and other conditions of ill health. These factors are continuously scrutinised in surveillance. Monitoring is one of the essential components of surveillance concept.

Objectives of surveillance are:

* To provide information about changing health trends

* To provide feedback which can change health policy

* To provide public health disaster warnings

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In cases of genital tuberculosis, which segment of the fallopian tube is frequently affected?
questions.explanation: Genital tuberculosis is a significant cause of tubal factor infertility in endemic regions, almost always involving the fallopian tubes bilaterally. Among the various segments of the fallopian tube, the ampulla (Option B) is the most frequently affected site. The infection typically begins in the mucosa and spreads to the other layers, leading to characteristic findings like "tobacco-pouch" or "beaded" appearances of the tubes on imaging. The isthmus (Option C) and infundibulum (Option A) are also involved as the disease progresses, but the ampulla's high vascularity and large surface area make it the primary site of initial colonization. The interstitium (Option D) is the least common primary site. Tuberculosis leads to chronic salpingitis and eventual tubal blockage, which is why it is a major focus in the evaluation of female infertility in the Indian subcontinent

questions.text:
According to IADPSG, what is the cut-off value of fasting blood glucose for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus?

IADPSG- International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Group
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. >92 mg/dL

According to IADPSG, the cut-off value of fasting blood glucose for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is >92 mg/dL.

Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) refers to any degree of glucose intolerance having its onset or first recognition during pregnancy.

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and GDM is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

• Fasting: >92 mg/dL
• 1hour: >180 mg/dL
• 2 hr: >153 mg/dL

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour OGTT is the diagnostic test for GDM. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive, as follows.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 1-week-old child was presented with early cataract. He also has refusal to feed, vomiting, lethargy, jaundice, and sepsis. This can be caused due to the deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase

Classic galactosemia is caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) and presents in neonates soon after milk feeding.

• Early cataract (due to galactitol accumulation in lens)
• Poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy
• Jaundice and hepatomegaly
• Failure to thrive
• Risk of E. coli sepsis

Biochemical basis:

• Block in conversion of galactose-1-phosphate → UDP-galactose
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate (toxic) and galactitol

Why not others:

• Aldose reductase deficiency: Would reduce cataract formation (not cause disease)
• Hexokinase: General glycolysis enzyme, not specific
• Catalase: Involved in oxidative stress, unrelated

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old truck driver presents with painful multiple ulcers on his penis 3 days after unprotected sexual intercourse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chancroid

Multiple painful genital ulcers 3 days after unprotected intercourse is indicative of Chancroid or Soft Chancre.

Chancroid is a type of sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It presents with painful genital ulceration along with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy that may develop into buboes. Auto-inoculation by the organism can result in new ulcers merging with the older ones. Hence, they are called "kissing ulcers."

The diagnosis is made clinically and can be supported by the school of fish/railroad track appearance on Gram stain (bacilli arranged in small groups, or parallel chains) as shown below:

First-line management is azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM in a single dose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with central chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia. The following changes were seen in the ECG. What is the most likely heart condition? MI - Myocardial infarction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterolateral wall MI

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with central chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia, and ECG showing convex type of ST elevation in lead 1, aVL, V2-6 with reciprocal changes (ST depression) in Lead 2, 3, aVF is consistent with Anterolateral wall MI.

MI occurs when there is severe cardiac muscle ischemia. Severe, acute ischemia causes a change in the membrane potential which shortens the duration of the action potential. This creates a voltage gradient between the normal myocardium and ischemic myocardium causing a flow of current between the two.  This altered flow of current manifests as changes in the ST segment, which represents ventricle repolarization. The change in the ST segment depends on the part of the myocardium involved.

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation.

* Administration of O2

* Give aspirin 325 mg and clopidogrel

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers.

* Give up to three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an afterload-reducing agent or loop diuretic.

* Give beta blockers if there are no features of heart failure.

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI.

In patients with STEMI, Reperfusion with Percutaneous coronary intervention(PCI) or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min). This is followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy.

In patients with NSTEMI, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is indicated.

Other options:

Option A: Acute pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium, also characterized by retrosternal chest pain that is aggravated by deep inspiration and a supine position and relieved by sitting and leaning forward. On auscultation, a pericardial friction rub is heard. On ECG, there is widespread concave type of elevation of the ST segments with depression of the PR segment.

Option C: Anterior Wall MI presents as ST elevation in lead V1-V4.

Option D: Inferior Wall MI presents as ST elevation in lead 2, 3, aVF with characteristic symptoms of Bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the hormones 1 and 2 in the following image
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1: Inhibin, 2: Testosterone

The image shows the Hypothalamic pituitary axis and the hormones 1 is Inhibin and 2 is testosterone.

Hypothalamus stimulates the Anterior pituitary via GnRh to release FSH and LH.

LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH by a negative feedback mechanism. FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to secrete inhibin, which in turn inhibits FSH by a negative feedback mechanism.

Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus. Inhibin acts directly on the anterior pituitary to inhibit FSH secretion.

FSH also stimulates the secretion of ABP (androgen-binding protein). FSH and androgens maintain the gametogenic function of the testes. Hypothalamic lesions in animals and hypothalamic disease in humans lead to atrophy of the testes and loss of their function.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young teenage boy presents to the emergency department with a history of drug use at a party a couple of hours earlier. He reports symptoms including sweating, headache, anxiety, and hyperactivity. On examination, he has tachycardia and hypertension. Which of the following substances could he have ingested? LSD-lysergic acid diethylamide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cocaine

Based on the clinical scenario provided, the substance the boy may have ingested is likely cocaine.

Cocaine is an alkaloid deliriant extracted from erythroxylum coca.

Acute intoxication with cocaine leads to symptoms spanning 2 stages :

* Stage of excitement/euphoria - associated with hypervigilance, anxiety, hyperactivity along with hyper-adrenergic signs of mydriasis, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmias.

* Stage of depression - associated with loss of reflexes, muscle paralysis, circulatory and respiratory failure, and coma.

Chronic intoxication is characterized by toxic delirium and tactile hallucination of bugs (cocaine bugs) or vermin crawling under the skin (formication).

Treatment includes intravenous diazepam for controlling seizures. For ventricular arrhythmias, propranolol may be given intravenously. If the patient has psychosis, haloperidol may be given. Treatment of chronic cocaine abuse requires psychiatric support.

Other options :

Option A: Shakes, hallucinations, and agitation are symptoms of alcohol withdrawal syndrome. They occur 12-24 hours following alcohol intake. Delirium tremens begin 72 to 96 hours after the last drink. It is due to the long-continued action of the poison on the brain. It occurs in chronic alcoholics due to temporary excess, sudden withdrawal of alcohol, shock after receiving an injury, such as fracture of a bone, or from acute infection, such as pneumonia, influenza, erysipelas, etc.

Option C:  Profuse sweating, diarrhea, and piloerection (gooseflesh) are symptoms of opioid withdrawal. They are associated with nausea, vomiting, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, muscle cramps, and generalized body aches. These symptoms manifest about 12-24 hours after the stoppage and recede within 7-10 days of last use.

Option D:  Synesthesia or seeing smells and hearing colors and flashback phenomenon (emotional and psychological experiences of the previous LSD) are features of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) intoxication. Other features include dry mouth, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, mood changes, visual hallucinations, alterations in time perceptions, vision, and hearing. Side effects are psychosis, depression, panic attacks, and schizophrenic episodes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child, upon disturbing a bee hive, had several stings. After a few minutes, the child developed symptoms of shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. Which of the following is the principal mediators of this reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histamine

Anaphylaxis following a bee sting is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or Type 1 hypersensitivity and the mediator involved here is histamine.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: ICER is used as an Economic model in which of the following Health Management Techniques:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cost effectiveness analysis

In health economics, decision makers often need to determine which health intervention provides the best value for money. One important method used for this purpose is Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA). It compared the cost of an intervention along with the health outcomes achieved.

ICER (Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio) is a key measure in cost-effectiveness analysis, used to compare the additional cost per additional unit of health outcome (e.g., cost per life-year or QALY gained) between two interventions. ICER is used for evaluating vaccination programs, cancer screening programs, new drug therapies, public health interventions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: After a roller coaster ride, a person experiences a brief sense of imbalance before standing upright. Which tract helps maintain balance in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vestibulospinal Tract

After a roller coaster ride, a person feels a slight imbalance and takes a minute to stand upright. The tract responsible for maintaining balance in this situation is the vestibulospinal tract.

Vestibular nuclei are situated in the pons and medulla oblongata beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. The vestibular nuclei receive afferent fibres from the inner ear through the vestibular nerve and from the cerebellum. Neurons of the lateral vestibular nucleus give rise to the axons that form the vestibulospinal tract. The tract descends uncrossed through the medulla and through the length of the spinal cord in the anterior white column. The fibres terminate by synapsing with internuncial neurons of the anterior grey column of the spinal cord.

The inner ear and the cerebellum, using this tract, facilitate the activity of the extensor muscles and inhibit the activity of the flexor muscles in association with the maintenance of balance.

Other options:

Option A: The tectospinal tract is a neural pathway that originates in the superior colliculus of the midbrain and plays a role in coordinating head and neck movements in response to visual and auditory stimuli. It helps orient the body toward visual or auditory sources of stimuli, contributing to reflexive head-turning.

Option B: The rubrospinal tract is a motor pathway that originates in the red nucleus of the midbrain and helps regulate voluntary movement, particularly in the upper limbs. It plays a role in facilitating flexor muscles and inhibiting extensor muscles, contributing to fine motor control.

Option D: The pyramidal tract, also known as the corticospinal tract, is a major pathway for voluntary motor control that originates in the cerebral cortex and travels through the brainstem. It is responsible for precise, skilled movements, particularly in the limbs and hands.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presented to a surgical emergency with complaints of severe epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, HR was 120/min and BP was 100/60 mm Hg. On palpation, there is tenderness, guarding and rigidity. What is the probable cause of the condition shown in the X-ray below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hollow viscus perforation

The clinical scenario of hypotension and tachycardia with abdominal tenderness, guarding and rigidity with free air under the diaphragm in X-ray is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.

Acute abdomen is a common surgical emergency. Common causes include appendicitis, hollow viscus perforation, cholecystitis, and pancreatitis. An erect abdominal X-ray is commonly done as the first investigation. Free air under the diaphragm can result from hollow viscus perforation including Gastric, duodenal, small bowel and large bowel perforations.

Causes of hollow viscus perforation are blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, infections(TB, typhoid, Crohn's), corrosive agents etc.

Clinical features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimation of the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel suggestive of paralytic ileus. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation mainly includes resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency exploratory laparotomy.

Other options: None of the other options have free air under the diaphragm.

Option A: Acute cholecystitis presents with pain in the right upper quadrant with fever and nausea. They may have tenderness and guarding. Rigidity is uncommon. Additionally, free air under the diaphragm may be seen in cases of gall bladder perforation only.

Option B: Sigmoid volvulus shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. On the x-ray abdomen, the apex of the sigmoid volvulus extends towards the right upper quadrant and the haustrations are usually lost.

Option D: In small bowel obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of fever, headache, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, she has neck stiffness and a positive Brudzinski’s sign. Lumbar puncture reveals cerebrospinal fluid with a markedly elevated white blood cell count predominantly composed of neutrophils, low glucose levels, and a positive latex agglutination test. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic clinical triad of meningitis: fever, headache, and meningeal signs such as Brudzinski’s sign. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is diagnostic and is consistent with acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis. Key CSF findings include a markedly elevated white blood cell count (>1000 cells/mm³) with neutrophil predominance and significantly reduced CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL or <50% of blood glucose). In addition, a positive latex agglutination test supports the diagnosis by detecting specific bacterial antigens, commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. Tubercular meningitis (Option B) and fungal meningitis (Option D) typically show lymphocytic pleocytosis, moderately reduced glucose, and a more subacute or chronic course. Viral meningitis (Option C) is characterized by normal CSF glucose, lymphocytic predominance, and a lower total WBC count. Therefore, the presence of neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose confirms a bacterial etiology, making Option A: Acute bacterial meningitis the definitive diagnosis. Immediate intravenous antibiotic therapy is essential to reduce morbidity and mortality

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs increases the uveoscleral outflow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Latanoprost

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin drug, which acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure.

Mechanism of action: Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles. This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases, which increases the uveoscleral outflow.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man after his retirement party came with the complaint of sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye for the past 2 hours. Fundoscopic examination shows a similar picture given below. What is the most probable cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CRAO

The given fundoscopic image shows a cherry-red spot, which is a feature of CRAO.

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk factors include

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Varicella infection

* Radiation exposure

* Trauma

Etiology:

* Emboli - emboli having carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are - cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

* Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

* Retinal arteritis with obliteration

* Angiospasm

* Raised intraocular pressure

* Thrombophilic disorders

Clinical features are

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Severe oedema- the whole retina looks white in colour

* Cherry red spots

* Marked attenuation of arteries – thread-like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in vein – cattle track appearance

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by I/V acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photo disruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presented with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. On examination, you note fixed, tender, retroverted uterus and tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometriosis

This patient presents with symptoms of dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea with a fixed retroverted uterus and tenderness in the pouch of Douglas most likely suffering from endometriosis.

For minimal disease, medical management with NSAIDs and oral contraceptive pills are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow. For moderate to severe diseases, oral progestogens, GnRH agonists or danazol that antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium causing endometrial atrophy are used.

Surgery is preferred in infertile women because hormonal treatment would delay pregnancy. Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser and resection of endometrioma can be done. Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) to control pain .Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a definitive and most effective therapy for women with endometriosis who do not wish to retain fertility.

Pearl PF1294: Endometriosis

Sites of Endometriosis:

* Pelvic endometriosis: Pelvic peritoneum, the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligament.

* Rectovaginal endometriosis.

* Ovarian endometriosis.

* Chocolate cyst of the ovary.

* Other sites—appendix, pelvic lymph nodes.

* Metastatic— lungs, umbilicus, scar endometriosis.

One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen.

Examination findings in endometriosis:

* Abdomen: Cystic swelling, fixed and tender.

* Pelvis: Cystic tender mass.

* Vaginal examination: Fixed, tender, retroverted uterus. Tenderness in the lateral fornices (indicative of endometriosis even if no mass).

* Speculum inspection of the Posterior fornix: Bluish/blackish puckered spots on speculum, tender to touch. The presence of puckered spots is pathognomonic of endometriosis.

* Posterior Fornix Palpation: Uterosacral ligaments & pouch of Douglas feel thickened and shotty with multiple small palpable nodules. This is called the cobblestone feel of uterosacral ligaments.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An infant presented in the surgical OPD with complaints of a unilateral swelling in the neck. The swelling was soft, cystic, partially compressible and brilliantly transilluminant. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic hygroma

Cystic hygroma (also called cystic lymphangioma) is a congenital lymphatic malformation that typically presents in infancy or early childhood as a soft, cystic, painless neck swelling. It is partially compressible and brilliantly transilluminant, making it the classic diagnosis in this scenario.

Why not other options?

• A. Branchial fistula:

• Presents as a persistent sinus or external opening along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle with intermittent discharge, not as a transilluminant cystic swelling.

• B. Branchial cyst

• Usually presents in older children or young adults as a painless lateral neck swelling.
• It is not brilliantly transilluminant.

• D. Thyroglossal cyst

• Presents as a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue.
• Usually not transilluminant.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: While discharging a patient who underwent a vesicovaginal fistula repair, which of the following would you recommend?
options: Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year
Sexual abstinence for 3 weeks and avoid pregnancy for 6 months
Sexual abstinence for 6 weeks and avoid pregnancy for a year
Sexual abstinence for 6 months and avoid pregnancy for 6 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year

While discharging a patient who underwent vesicovaginal fistula repair, sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoiding pregnancy for a year would be recommended.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of urinary fistula which commonly arises due to obstetric trauma. Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside. Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Presenting features of VVF include constant dribbling of urine/ true incontinence. Excoriation of the vagina, vulva, and thighs can occur due to constant contact with urine. Few patients might develop bladder stones. Vaginal urine collection can be seen on retraction of the posterior vaginal wall with a speculum. A bimanual examination can be used to assess the fixity and scarring of the surrounding tissues. A cystourethroscopy can be used for localization and assessing bladder mucosa viability.
questions.learning: Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year While discharging a patient who underwent vesicovaginal fistula repair, sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoiding pregnancy for a year would be recommended.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following are the tools used for classification of spasticity in a child with cerebral palsy? I. Gross Motor Function Classification System II. Medical Research Council System III. Modified Connors Scale (Connors-II) IV. Modified Ashworth Scale Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and IV

Assessment of children with cerebral palsy (CP) involves evaluating both functional motor ability and muscle spasticity. The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) classifies gross motor function, while the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) is the most commonly used clinical tool to grade spasticity.

Why is D correct?

• I. Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) ✔

• Classifies gross motor function in children with CP into five levels (I–V) based on self-initiated movement, sitting, walking, and mobility.
• It is the standard functional classification system in cerebral palsy.

• II. Medical Research Council (MRC) System ✘

• Used to assess muscle strength (power), not spasticity.

• III. Modified Connors Scale (Conners-II) ✘

• Used for assessment of ADHD symptoms, not cerebral palsy or spasticity.

• IV. Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) ✔

• Grades muscle spasticity by assessing resistance to passive movement.
• It is the most widely used clinical scale for spasticity.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: How do local anesthetics function?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics such as lignocaine (lidocaine) and bupivacaine act by reversibly blocking voltage-gated Na⁺ channels on the inner surface of the neuronal membrane. By preventing the influx of Na⁺ ions, they inhibit membrane depolarization, thereby blocking the initiation and propagation of action potentials. As a result, pain impulses cannot be transmitted from the peripheral nerves to the central nervous system. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Potassium (K⁺) channels regulate repolarization, not impulse initiation. 2. Calcium (Ca²⁺) channels are involved in neurotransmitter release at synapses. 3. Chloride (Cl⁻) channels mainly mediate inhibitory neurotransmission
questions.learning: Local anesthetics such as lignocaine (lidocaine) and bupivacaine act by reversibly blocking voltage-gated Na⁺ channels on the inner surface of the neuronal membrane.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Magnesium sulphate has no role in:
options: Prevention of seizures in severe pre-eclampsia
Prevention of recurrent seizures in eclampsia
Prevention of RDS in premature baby
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prevention of RDS in premature baby

Magnesium sulfate has no role in the prevention of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in a premature baby, where there is a deficit of surfactant (which results in alveolar collapse).

Magnesium in the MgSO4 competes with calcium on voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby altering its uptake and release. Functions of MgSO4 include :

• Membrane protector and neuro stabilizer. It is used in the prevention of cerebral palsy in very low birth weight neonates.
• Reduction of motor endplate sensitivity to acetylcholine, and thus is used as an adjunct in the management of acute severe asthma in children and adults
• Blocking of neuronal calcium influx, and is thus used in the conservative management of pre-term labor (tocolytic, option D)
• Inducing cerebral vasodilatation, dilating the uterine arteries, increasing the production of endothelial prostacyclin, and inhibiting platelet activation. Hence it is used in the management of pre-eclampsia (option A) and to prevent progression to eclampsia (option A).
questions.learning: Prevention of RDS in premature baby Magnesium sulfate has no role in the prevention of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in a premature baby, where there is a deficit of surfactant (which results in alveolar collapse).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with multiple freckles, severe photosensitivity, and early-onset skin cancers. What is the primary underlying molecular defect responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleotide excision repair defect

The clinical features—multiple freckles, severe photosensitivity, and early-onset skin cancers—are characteristic of Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP).

Underlying molecular defect:

• Defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway
• This pathway normally repairs UV-induced DNA damage, especially pyrimidine (thymine) dimers

Pathophysiology:

• UV radiation → formation of thymine dimers
• NER defect → inability to remove damaged DNA
• Accumulation of mutations → high risk of skin cancers at an early age

Why other options are incorrect:

• Mismatch repair defect: Seen in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
• Base excision repair defect: Repairs small base damage (oxidation, deamination)
• Homologous recombination defect: Seen in BRCA mutations (breast/ovarian cancer)
questions.learning: Nucleotide excision repair defect — The clinical features—multiple freckles, severe photosensitivity, and early-onset skin cancers—are characteristic of Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient was brought to the hospital after a road traffic accident. He had severe muscle injury and his serum K+ level was found to be 5.5 mEq/L. What change will happen to the resting membrane potential in this patient?
options: First becomes more positive, then negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Becomes more positive

Hyperkalemia reduces the K⁺ gradient across the cell membrane, decreasing outward K⁺ diffusion. This makes the resting membrane potential less negative (partial depolarization). As extracellular K⁺ rises, the membrane shifts toward threshold. Hence the resting membrane potential becomes more positive.

↓

↓ Concentration gradient

↓

↓ K⁺ efflux from cell

↓

Less positive charge leaving

↓

Inside becomes less negative

↓

RMP shifts toward zero (more positive)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After starting CPR on a person who has collapsed following a road traffic accident and once the rescue team arrives, what is the most appropriate next action to take?
options: Continue 5 rounds of CPR @ 30:2 followed by application of an AED
Continue CPR while the team applies AED paddles
Stop CPR and let them apply paddles
questions.explanation: In advanced cardiac life support, minimizing interruptions in chest compressions is vital for maintaining coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure. When a rescue team arrives with an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) while a bystander is performing CPR, the rescuer should continue high-quality chest compressions without stopping while the team prepares the device and applies the paddles or pads to the patient’s chest. Stopping CPR prematurely (Option C) reduces the chances of successful resuscitation. Waiting to complete exactly five rounds (Option A) is unnecessary if the AED is ready for immediate use, as early rhythm analysis is prioritized. Simply handing over and leaving (Option D) is inappropriate until a formal transfer of care is complete and the rescuer is no longer needed to assist. The core principle is that compressions should only pause when the AED explicitly prompts "analyzing" or "clear for shock" to maximize the patient's survival probability

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a blast injury, which of the following organs is least vulnerable to the blast wave?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Liver

In a blast injury, the liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT.

The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes > lungs. Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion.

Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure.

Classification of blast injuries:

Classification
Explanation
Injury type
Examples

Primary blast
Due to air pressure from the blast
Shockwave (overpressure)
Tympanic membrane injury, blast lung, intestinal blast injury

Secondary blast
Fragments from the blast, following a detonation
Penetrating/fragmentation
All penetrating injuries

Tertiary blast
Gross movements of persons, objects, or infrastructure by the blast wind
Blunt trauma
Blunt and crush injuries. Traumatic amputation.

Quaternary blast
Miscellaneous causes
Exposure to explosive products or toxic substances
Burns, inhalation injury

Quinary blast
The intentional addition of biological or radioactive material to the explosive device
Environmental contaminants
Radiation sickness, infection.
questions.learning: Liver — In a blast injury, the liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury. Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a perineal approach for the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ripstein's procedure

The condition shown in the image is a rectal prolapse and Ripstein's procedure is done using the abdominal approach.

Rectal prolapse occurs when a mucosal or full-thickness layer of rectal tissue protrudes through the anal orifice. Rectal prolapse is of two types:

• Partial rectal prolapse: Only the mucosal layer of the rectum is prolapsed. It is seen in children.
• Complete rectal prolapse:  All the layers of the rectum are prolapsed. It is seen in adults due to the weakening of the pelvic floor.

Management:

• The first episode of a partial rectal prolapse is managed by digital repositioning. On recurrence, Theirsch's wiring or sclerotherapy are considered.
• Complete rectal prolapse is managed surgically, either by perineal or abdominal approaches:

1. Perineal approach: Often preferred in patients with high operative risk and limited life expectancy, i.e. in the elderly. It is associated with less morbidity but has a higher recurrence rate.

• Thiersch's wiring- A steel wire/nylon tape is placed around the anal canal. Largely obsolete now due to problems with chronic perineal sepsis, anal stenosis, and obstructed defecation.
• Delorme's mucosectomy- The rectal mucosa is stripped circumferentially from the rectum over the length of the prolapse. The underlying muscle is plicated with a series of sutures. The excess rectal mucosa is excised and a mucosal anastomosis is performed.
• Altemeier's rectosigmoidectomy- The rectum is prolapsed through the anal canal and a full-thickness resection is performed, incorporating any associated colonic prolapse. Restoration of colorectal continuity can be performed by hand-sewn/stapled anastomosis. This is the procedure of choice in patients presenting with incarcerated and strangulated prolapse.

2. Abdominal approach: Difficult to perform, more complications but a lower recurrence rate.

• Ripstein's procedure- involves the placement of a prosthetic mesh around the mobilized rectum, with the attachment of the mesh to the presacral fascia (anterior) below the sacral promontory.
• Well's procedure- involves posterior rectopexy.
• Suture rectopexy
questions.learning: Ripstein's procedure — The condition shown in the image is a rectal prolapse and Ripstein's procedure is done using the abdominal approach. Rectal prolapse occurs when a mucosal or full-thickness layer of rectal tissue protrudes through the anal orifice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following steps of disaster management is in correct order?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation

The steps of disaster management are Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation.

Disaster Management includes three aspects:

1. Disaster impact and response:

Involves immediate management of mass casualties

* Search, rescue, and first-aid

* Field care

* Triage

* Tagging

* Identification of dead

2. Rehabilitation or recovery:

Involves restoration of the pre-disaster conditions

* Water supply

* Basic sanitation and personal hygiene

* Food safety

* Vector control

3. Mitigation: Measures designed either to prevent hazards from causing disaster or to reduce the effects of the disaster. This also includes preparedness for any impending disasters or in disaster-prone areas.
questions.learning: Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation The steps of disaster management are Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a focal non-cicatricial cause of alopecia? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Discoid Lupus Erythematosus

Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is a cicatricial (scarring) alopecia, making it the exception among the options listed. Chronic inflammation destroys hair follicles and replaces them with fibrous tissue, resulting in permanent hair loss.

In contrast, the following are causes of focal non-cicatricial alopecia, where hair follicles remain intact and regrowth is possible:

• Alopecia areata – autoimmune attack on hair follicles causing smooth, well-circumscribed patches of hair loss.
• Secondary syphilis – causes characteristic “moth-eaten” patchy alopecia.
• Black dot tinea capitis – fungal infection causing hair shaft breakage at the scalp surface, leaving black dots.

Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia = permanent follicular destruction

• DLE
• Lichen planopilaris
• Folliculitis decalvans

Non-scarring alopecia = follicles preserved

• Alopecia areata
• Tinea capitis
• Telogen effluvium
• Secondary syphilis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient with a long-standing history of smoking presents with complaints of dysphagia. Based on this clinical scenario, which type of lung cancer is most commonly associated with such a presentation?
questions.explanation: In a male chronic smoker presenting with dysphagia, the clinical suspicion points toward a central lung tumor that is compressing the esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A) is the type of lung cancer most strongly associated with smoking and is classically located in a central (hilar) position. Because of its central location, it is the most likely subtype to cause extrinsic compression of the esophagus, leading to the patient's difficulty swallowing. Adenocarcinoma (Option B) is the most common lung cancer overall but is typically located peripherally and is less specifically linked to heavy smoking compared to the squamous type. Large cell carcinoma (Option C) is also often peripheral. "Bronchogenic carcinoma" (Option D) is a general term for all primary lung cancers rather than a specific pathological subtype. Therefore, given the specific combination of smoking history and central compressive symptoms, Squamous cell carcinoma is the expected predominant diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old morbidly obese male patient presented with complaints of severe abdominal pain and urinary disturbances. His urine microscopy shows the following type of crystals and an ultrasound of the kidney revealed a renal stone of size 2.5 cm. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)

Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, typical of cystine stones that are radio-opaque (due to high sulfur content). The treatment of choice for renal calculi of size 2.5 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

Indications of PCNL:

* Staghorn calculi

* Stones >2 cm in size

* Stone composition - struvite, calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones

* Multiple stones

* Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated

* Stones not responding for ESWL

Endoscopic instruments are passed into the kidney using a percutaneous technique and stones are removed.

Complications of percutaneous nephrolithotomy include:

* Haemorrhage from the punctured renal parenchyma

* Perforation of the collecting system with extravasation of saline irrigant

* Perforation of the colon or pleural cavity during placement of the percutaneous track

Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy:

ESWL is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the commonest method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 2 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.Cystine stones are very hard stones as a result of disulphide bonds and do not fragment with ESWL. Other stones that are difficult to disintegrate by ESWL include cystine, brushite, and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones.

ESWL is only 45-60% effective in the treatment of large stones. It causes frequent complications including pain, hydronephrosis, fever, and occasional urosepsis, due to difficulties in the passage of stone particles, especially in cases of insufficient disintegration.

Complications: Infection, haematuria, parenchymal haemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma.

Contraindications: Obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Stone fragments collecting in the distal ureter following ESWL are called steinstrasse  (a german word, which means 'street of stones'). The most common site of the column of stone fragments obstruction is the distal ureter, followed by the proximal ureter and mid ureter. The postoperative image is attached below.

Ureteroscopic removal: Ureteric calculi are directly visualized through semi-rigid ureteroscopes. Stones are then fragmented and extracted using a dormia basket.

These are generally preferred for stones <6mm and specifically those present in the distal ureter. The most significant complications relate to injury to the ureteric mucosa or wall and include ureteric perforation and extravasation, avulsion of the ureter and ureteric stricture.

Open surgery: A longstanding obstructing calculus can result in chronic inflammatory change in the kidney. Open surgeries are generally indicated for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP). Generally, in such cases, a subcapsular nephrectomy is performed.

In extremely rare cases where both PCNL and ESWL are contraindicated open/laparoscopic surgery is used.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing for both solids and liquids for 8 months. Barium swallow done is shown below. What other investigations need to be done in this patient?
options: Upper GI endoscopy and 24 hour PH monitoring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper GI endoscopy & Manometry

The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing a bird beak appearance are suggestive of achalasia cardia.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing.

Manometry is considered the most sensitive investigation to diagnose achalasia as it identifies early disease before esophageal dilatation and food retention. The diagnostic criteria for achalasia with manometry are impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis with an elevated LES pressure.

Endoscopy is useful for ruling out pseudo-achalasia.

Note: 24-hour pH monitoring is ideal and most accurate in patients with the features of gastroesophageal reflux disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 84-year-old man with a history of stroke 2 years ago, who is on prolonged bed rest, develops a pressure ulcer with partial thickness skin loss and a clean base. What is the grade of his pressure sore?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grade 2

The pressure sore is of grade 2 in this case.

Grade 2 of bedsore corresponds to partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis.

Pressure sores, also known as bedsores, pressure ulcers, or decubitus ulcers, are defined as tissue necrosis with ulceration due to prolonged pressure. When the external pressure exceeds the capillary occlusive pressure, blood flow ceases leading to tissue anoxia, necrosis, and ulceration. An external pressure of >30 mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores.

The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are the ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral followed by medial), and occiput.

Given below are images showing the stages of pressure sore.

Prevention is the best treatment for pressure sores. They can be prevented with good skincare, the use of air-fluidized beds, special pressure-dispersion cushions, or foams. Fecal or urinary diversion can be considered in special cases.

The position of the bedridden patients should be changed once every 2 hours and wheel-chair bound patients should be taught to get off their chairs for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgical management of pressure sores follows the same principles involved in acute wound treatment. Prior to the operation, the pressure sores should be adequately debrided, and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) can be used to promote the growth of granulation tissue required for surgical closure. Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction.

VAC is done by applying intermittent negative pressure of approximately -125 mmHg to hasten debridement and promote granulation tissue formation. Negative pressure decreases edema, removes interstitial fluid, and increases blood flow. This decreases bacterial growth and increases cell proliferation.
questions.learning: Grade 2 — The pressure sore is of grade 2 in this case. Grade 2 of bedsore corresponds to partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following features are not associated with the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Munro microabscesses

The image shows characteristic lesions of Lichen Planus and Munro microabscesses are not a feature of Lichen Planus but seen in Psoriasis.

Lichen planus (LP) is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane.

Patients present with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae. They are commonly seen on the volar aspect of the wrists, the lumbar region, and around the ankles.

The mucosal involvement is also seen. The commonest mucosal sites are buccal mucosa and tongue, rarely it can also be found on the buccal mucosa, anus, genitalia, etc.

Nail involvement can be seen as thinning of nail plate leading to an exaggeration of longitudinal lines, and linear depressions. The nails can also be destroyed leading to anonychia. Involvement of nail bed may give rise to longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis.

Microscopy will show acanthosis of the epidermis, irregular thickening of the granular layer, and compact hyperkeratosis.  Degenerating basal epidermal cells are transformed into colloid bodies. The rete ridges can display a sawtooth pattern, and localized detachment from the dermis may form Max Joseph spaces. Active lichen planus is characterised by infiltration of lymphocytes arranged in the form of a band at the junction between the dermis and epidermis.

Other options:

Munro microabscess is the accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. The lesions present as red scaly plaques which are well demarcated with the surrounding normal skin. They might have a circle of clear zone around it which is known as the Woronoff ring.

Pearl PF1438: Nail changes in lichen planus

Nail involvement in lichen planus occurs in up to 10% of the cases but is usually a minor feature of the disease.

Dorsal Nail Pterygium is the most specific nail change in Lichen planus. The fusion of dorsal nail fold and nail bed leads to pterygium.

The most frequent nail change is the exaggeration of longitudinal lines and linear depressions due to a slight thinning of the nail plate.

Pup-tent sign - elevation of nail in shape of tent

Trachonychia - 20 nail dystrophy

Subungual Hyperkeratosis and Onycholysis

Longitudinal Melanonychia in Lichen Planus of the nail bed

Permanent destruction of several toenails with ulceration of soles (rare variant)

Image shows  Nails in Lichen planus presented with irregular longitudinal grooves and ridges .

Image : Dorsal Nail Pterygium

Image : Pup-tent sign

Image : Trachonychia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with diarrhea is diagnosed with cholera. The causative agent acts on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GM1 ganglioside receptor

Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae and the toxin produced by this organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors.

Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility. It has a single polar flagellum. It causes cholera, an acute diarrheal disease. It is marked by painless, profuse, watery diarrhea with flecks of mucus (rice water stools) associated with effortless vomiting. Pulmonary edema and arrhythmias are some of the complications.

Infection is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food and water. The organisms produce an enterotoxin known as cholera toxin (CT). It has 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B subunit (binding units) fixes to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on jejunal epithelial cells. The A subunit dissociates into the A2 fragment, which attaches the A1 fragment to the B subunit. This results in prolonged accumulation of cAMP, which causes an outpouring of large amounts of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Ultimately, it results in profuse watery diarrhea.

In addition to the cholera toxin, additional toxins such as zona occludens toxin and accessory cholera toxin are also produced. The former alters intestinal permeability by its action on intestinal epithelial cells.

The characteristic darting mobility and its hindrance by antiserum can be used for rapid microscopic diagnosis.

Fluid resuscitation by rice-based ORS is recommended. Medical management includes erythromycin or azithromycin.

Other options:

* GM2 gangliosides are involved in the metabolism of gangliosides, and abnormalities in their metabolism can lead to diseases like Tay-Sachs disease.

* The Gi protein-coupled receptor is a type of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that plays a role in signal transduction. They are involved in a wide range of physiological processes, including cell signaling and responses to various hormones and neurotransmitters.

* GM3 gangliosides are another type of glycosphingolipid found in cell membranes, and are involved in various cellular processes.
questions.learning: GM1 ganglioside receptor Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae and the toxin produced by this organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors. Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman noticed a neck swelling 2 months back. Clinical examination reveals a solitary nodule on the right side as shown. What is the most appropriate initial investigation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum TSH, T3 and T4

This patient is presenting with thyroid swelling along with image given is suggestive of Solitary Thyroid Nodule. Assessing the biochemical function of the thyroid, i.e. thyroid function test (TFT) which includes serum TSH, T3, and T4 is the first investigation done on any thyroid condition.

Investigations in a patient with Solitary thyroid nodule

• Thyroid function tests- Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels are the first step in evaluating suspected thyroid disease. Based on TSH levels, further investigations is decided.
• Ultrasonography is a non-invasive and inexpensive way to stratify the risk of the nodule into benign or malignant tissue.
• FNAC: Although other investigations can assist in evaluating a nodule, FNA cytology provides a definitive diagnosis.
• Radioiodine Thyroid scan: It helps to differentiate between a hot nodule and a cold nodule. Thyroid nodules that absorb radioiodine are called hot nodules. These nodules produce excess thyroid hormones and are functional nodules. Whereas, the thyroid nodules that do not absorb radioiodine are called cold nodules and they indicate non-functional nodules. It is mostly done by I-123 radioisotope. (Option C)

Other options:

Option A: I-131 radioisotope is more commonly used to radio-ablate the thyroid tissue.

Option B: PET scan has no role in the evaluation of Solitary thyroid nodules.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman 3 months postpartum who regularly breastfeeds presented with amenorrhea for 3 months and is concerned about this problem and is requesting surgery. Before considering surgery what can be done to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reassure

The best management of this patient is to reassure her as this is normal during postpartum and is due to lactactional amenorrhea.

Lactactional amenorrhea:

* Type of secondary amenorrhea due to the effect or prolactin secretion.

* During lactation, there are pulsatile bursts of prolactin secretion in response to suckling.

* Prolactin suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH causing lactational amenorrhea.

* Regular lactation with one feed at night delays ovulation and pregnancy for up to 6 months, provided she remains amenorrhoeic.

* After 6 months, lactation has no bearing on ovulation and pregnancy can occur, despite amenorrhoea and might need other forms of contraception.

Other options:

Oral combined pill in a lactating woman is contraindicated because:

* It reduces the quality and quantity of milk.

* The hormone in the milk may be harmful to the infant.

* Increased risk of thromboembolism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain four days after undergoing a cholecystectomy. Ultrasonography reveals a significant fluid collection in the right upper quadrant. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: USG-guided aspiration of content In a stable patient presenting with a localized fluid collection post-cholecystectomy, the immediate next step is USG-guided aspiration. This is essential to confirm the nature of the fluid—specifically distinguishing between a bile leak (biloma), an abscess (pus), or a hematoma (blood). Identifying the fluid type directly guides subsequent steps; for example, if bile is found, an MRCP or ERCP (Option C) would then be indicated to locate and treat the leak. Re-exploration (Option A) is overly invasive as an initial step. While antibiotics (Option B) may be started, they cannot replace the diagnostic and therapeutic necessity of drainage. Therefore, aspiration is the most appropriate and conservative first-line diagnostic intervention.
questions.learning: USG-guided aspiration of content — In a stable patient presenting with a localized fluid collection post-cholecystectomy, the immediate next step is USG-guided aspiration.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with foul-smelling bloody discharge per vagina mixed with mucous discharge. On examination, a necrotizing growth is seen in the cervix with lateral parametrium involvement. What will be the management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chemoradiation

Lateral parametrium involvement = FIGO Stage IIB carcinoma cervix. Standard of care from Stage IIB onwards is concurrent chemoradiation (external beam + brachytherapy). Surgery is reserved for earlier stages (up to 2A1). For Stage IIB cervical cancer, the treatment of choice is: Concurrent chemoradiation

This involves:

| Treatment | Purpose

| --------- | -------

| External beam radiotherapy | Destroy tumor

| Cisplatin | Enhances radiation effect

| Brachytherapy | Internal radiation

Once parametrium is involved, surgical removal becomes difficult because:

Tumor extends into parametrium

↓

Cannot obtain clear surgical margins

↓

Higher recurrence risk

Thus chemoradiation is preferred.
questions.learning: Chemoradiation Lateral parametrium involvement = FIGO Stage IIB carcinoma cervix. Standard of care from Stage IIB onwards is concurrent chemoradiation (external beam + brachytherapy).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 74 year old gentleman presents to the OPD with history of significant unintentional weight loss, loss of appetite and iron deficiency anemia. A chest x-ray was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metastasis

The above scenario indicates the patient may be suffering from colon carcinoma. The X-ray depicts cannon ball appearance classical of lung metastasis.
Pulmonary metastasis typically appears as peripheral, rounded nodules of variable size, scattered throughout both lungs. The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
questions.learning: Metastasis — The above scenario indicates the patient may be suffering from colon carcinoma. The X-ray depicts cannon ball appearance classical of lung metastasis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text:
A patient who is a chronic alcoholic presents with seizures and altered sensorium. He has been drinking for the past 10 years and takes 24 units per day. His last drink was 2 days back. He is found to have auditory hallucinations and secondary delusions. What will you use for the management of this patient?

1. Diazepam
2. Thiamine
3. Naltrexone
4. Flupenthixol depot injection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1,2

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of delirium tremens. Management of this patient involves the administration of diazepam and thiamine.

Delirium tremens is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal syndrome. It occurs usually within 3–4 days of alcohol withdrawal.

Characteristic features of delirium tremens:

• Clouding of consciousness, with disorientation to time and place
• Poor attention and distractibility
• Visual hallucinations and illusions, which are often vivid and very frightening
• Autonomic disturbances like tachycardia, fever, hypertension, diaphoresis, and pupillary dilatation
• Psychomotor agitation and ataxia

Benzodiazepines such as diazepam (intravenously) or chlordiazepoxide (orally every 4 hours) are given. It is also recommended to administer thiamine in patients with alcohol-related disorders to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Acute alcohol intoxication can be treated with the evacuation of stomach and bowel and gastric lavage with an alkaline solution. Administration of 1 L of normal saline with 10% glucose, 100 mg thiamine, and 15 U insulin may be useful. If the coma progresses deeper, stimulants like strychnine and caffeine can be used. Patients should be started on artificial respiration if there is respiratory depression or difficulty breathing.

Chronic alcohol intoxication can be treated with disulfiram (daily dose of 250 mg OD), conditioned reflex treatment, hypnosis, and psychotherapy.

According to the Motor Vehicle Amendment bill (2019), whoever while driving, or attempting to drive, a motor vehicle, has, in his/her blood, alcohol exceeding 30 mg/100 mL of blood, detected in a test by a breath analyzer, is punishable by law.

Naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist which is used along with cognitive behavioral therapy in cases of opioid withdrawal and alcohol withdrawal. It reduces craving and consumption, also reduces the severity of withdrawal symptoms.

Flupenthixol is an antipsychotic antagonist of both D1 and D2 dopamine receptors. The depot injections are used for the management of schizophrenia and depression.
questions.learning: 1,2 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of delirium tremens. Management of this patient involves the administration of diazepam and thiamine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Scientists studying the kidney's response to hypoperfusion apply a clip to a pig's right renal artery that reduces blood flow to the kidney by about 7 %. After 6 months, they perform a right nephrectomy and examine the glomeruli and tubules microscopically. Which of the following cell types would be most likely to undergo hyperplasia as a result of the clip placement?
options: Cuboidal epithelial cells of the proximal tubules
Endothelial cells of the efferent arteriole
Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole

Chronic renal hypoperfusion (as in renal artery stenosis/Goldblatt model) stimulates increased renin secretion.

Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole. Persistent decreased renal blood flow leads to hyperplasia and hypertrophy of JG cells due to sustained RAAS activation.

Thus, chronic hypoperfusion causes proliferation of modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole.
questions.learning: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole Chronic renal hypoperfusion (as in renal artery stenosis/Goldblatt model) stimulates increased renin secretion.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following causes an increase in ACh release from the presynaptic neuron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Potassium channel blocker

Potassium channel blockers cause an increase in ACh release from the presynaptic neuron.

Presynaptic potassium channel block promotes the activation of voltage-gated calcium channels. This leads to a release of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction.

Aminopyridines (K+ channel blockers) are used in the treatment of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome which helps to improve muscle strength.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person who was mentally unsound at the time of committing a crime is exempt from legal liability if they were unaware of the nature of their actions or their consequences. What is this legal principle called?
questions.explanation: The McNaughton rule (or M'Naghten rule) is the foundational legal principle for the insanity defense. It states that a person is not criminally responsible for their actions if, at the time of the offense, a "defect of reason" from a disease of the mind made them unaware of the nature and quality of the act or, if they did know it, that they did not know it was wrong. Durham's rule (Option B) is a broader, less common standard stating that a person is not responsible if their act was the "product" of a mental disease. Currens rule (Option C) relates to the "substantial capacity" to conform one's conduct to the law. The Irresistible impulse test (Option D) focuses on whether a person had the power to control their actions, even if they knew they were wrong. The McNaughton rule remains the most widely used standard in many legal systems, including India (Section 84 of the IPC), as it places the focus on the cognitive ability of the individual at the exact moment of the crime
