questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presented with post-menopausal bleeding. Ultrasonography revealed a mass with feeding vessel as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial polyp

Visualization of a mass with a single feeding vessel on a color Doppler is characteristic of an endometrial polyp.  In contrast, submucous leiomyomas often receive blood flow from multiple vessels (option A).

Endometrial polyps are soft, fleshy growths within the uterus that consist of endometrial glands, fibrous stroma, and surface epithelium. Risk factors for endometrial polyps include increasing age, obesity, and tamoxifen use.

They are usually asymptomatic. When symptomatic, they present with heavy menstrual bleeding, prolonged bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, or infertility.

The main diagnostic tools for endometrial polyps include transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) with applied color Doppler, saline infusion sonography, and hysteroscopy.

The risk factors for the malignant transformation include postmenopausal status, age older than 60, and abnormal bleeding. Other factors such as larger polyp size (>1.5 cm), tamoxifen use, diabetes, and obesity may also contribute to a higher risk.

Hysteroscopic polypectomy may be considered most effective for symptomatic women or those with risk factors for malignant transformation.
questions.learning: Endometrial polyp Visualization of a mass with a single feeding vessel on a color Doppler is characteristic of an endometrial polyp. In contrast, submucous leiomyomas often receive blood flow from multiple vessels (option A).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the obstetric grip being depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the Fourth Leopold manoeuvre, also known as the Pelvic Grip. In this manoeuvre, the clinician faces the mother's feet and places their hands on either side of the lower uterine segment just above the pelvic inlet. Its primary purpose is to determine the degree of fetal head engagement and to identify the fetal "brow" or "occiput" (the cephalic prominence). Fundal grip (Option C, First manoeuvre) involves palpating the upper uterus while facing the mother. Umbilical grip (Option D, Second manoeuvre) involves palpating the fetal back and limbs on either side of the abdomen. The Third manoeuvre (Pawlik's grip) involves a single hand over the symphysis. Hudsons grip (Option B) is not a standard obstetric term. The specific orientation of the clinician facing the feet while assessing the pelvic contents identifies this as the fourth manoeuvre. It is the final step in the clinical assessment of fetal lie and presentation
questions.learning: The image depicts the Fourth Leopold manoeuvre, also known as the Pelvic Grip. In this manoeuvre, the clinician faces the mother's feet and places their hands on either side of the lower uterine segment just above the pelvic inlet.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female singer with hoarseness of voice, unable to sing higher frequency notes. Bowed and depressed unilateral vocal cord is seen. Which muscle is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cricothyroid

The cricothyroid muscle is the primary tensor of the vocal cords, responsible for increasing pitch (high-frequency sound production).

• Action: Tilts thyroid cartilage forward → stretches & tenses vocal cords
• Function: Enables high-pitched sounds (singing high notes)
• Nerve supply: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve (SLN)
• Hoarseness + inability to sing high notes → loss of vocal cord tension

Suggests cricothyroid muscle paralysis

Why not other options:

• Posterior cricoarytenoid: Only abductor of vocal cords → affects airway, not pitch
• Thyroarytenoid: Relaxes vocal cords → affects low pitch, not high pitch loss
• Interarytenoid: Adducts vocal cords → affects closure, not tension

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with weakness of the face, arm, and leg on the side opposite to the lesion. Non-contrast CT of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. What is the most likely anatomical location of the bleed?
questions.explanation: Intracerebral hemorrhages (ICH) that result in dense contralateral hemiparesis (weakness of the face, arm, and leg) most commonly occur in the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen. Bleeding in this region compresses the adjacent internal capsule, through which the corticospinal fibers pass, leading to widespread motor deficits on the opposite side of the body. Midbrain lesions (Option B) often cause oculomotor nerve palsies in addition to motor weakness but are less common sites for primary ICH. Pontine hemorrhages (Option C) frequently result in quadriplegia or "locked-in" syndrome rather than simple hemiparesis. Medullary hemorrhages (Option D) are rare and typically present with contralateral limb weakness combined with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits (Wallenberg syndrome). Given the classic presentation of hemi-weakness, the basal ganglia is the most statistically and clinically likely location
questions.learning: Intracerebral hemorrhages (ICH) that result in dense contralateral hemiparesis (weakness of the face, arm, and leg) most commonly occur in the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following organizations does not contribute funding to India’s National Tuberculosis Control Programme?
questions.explanation: India's National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP) is a massive public health initiative supported by several major domestic and international entities. The Government of India (Option A) provides the primary budgetary support. Major external funding and technical assistance come from the World Bank (Option B) through development credits and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (Option C). UNICEF (Option D), while a vital partner in child health and nutrition, is not a primary funding source for the adult-centric national TB elimination program. The NTEP aims to eliminate TB in India by 2025, which is five years ahead of the global Sustainable Development Goal. Funding is directed toward providing free diagnostics, medications, and nutritional support (Nikshay Poshan Yojana) to all TB patients. Understanding the financial stakeholders is important for program management, as these organizations also monitor the progress and quality of TB services
questions.learning: India's National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP) is a massive public health initiative supported by several major domestic and international entities.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) presents to the outpatient department with seizures. On further examination and evaluation, homonymous hemianopia and epilepsy are noted. Based on the CT scan provided, identify the most likely diagnosis.
questions.explanation: The patient's history of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) followed by seizures and homonymous hemianopia strongly suggests a temporal lobe abscess. A brain abscess is a dangerous complication of CSOM, resulting from the direct spread of infection through the thin tegmen tympani. Seizures occur due to cortical irritation, while homonymous hemianopia indicates that the abscess is compressing the optic radiations (Meyer's loop) which pass through the temporal lobe. A cerebellar abscess (Option B) typically presents with ataxia and vertigo rather than seizures or visual field defects. An extradural abscess (Option C) causes severe localized pain but usually lacks focal neurological signs like hemianopia. Meningitis (Option D) presents with global signs like neck stiffness and altered mental status but not a localized ring-enhancing mass on CT. Prompt neurosurgical intervention and high-dose antibiotics are required for management
questions.learning: The patient's history of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) followed by seizures and homonymous hemianopia strongly suggests a temporal lobe abscess.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with a habit of biting his lips and fingers and you observe missing portions of fingers on his left hand. A detailed evaluation reveals delayed developmental milestone.On inquiry, the parents say that two male cousins on the mother's side have similar complaints and have been diagnosed with a genetic disorder. Lab reports reveal hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase

The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It occurs due to the complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT).

Purines can be converted to nucleoside triphosphates to be reused by the body. This pathway is called the salvage pathway for purines.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). This causes increased de novo purine synthesis and excessive amounts of uric acid.

The clinical features include compulsive self-mutilation, intellectual disability, delayed milestones, dystonic movements, and hyperuricemia.

Diagnosis is made by deficient HGPRT enzyme activity in the erythrocyte.

The treatment of this condition includes:

* Allopurinol for hyperuricemia

* Behavioral management using restraints for self-mutilation

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Other options:

Option A:  Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency results in decreased function of T cells but B cells are normal. This leads to multiple infections, neurologic abnormalities, and autoimmune diseases.

Option C: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency results in the accumulation of adenine. This is oxidized to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine which is insoluble. This leads to urinary calculus formation with crystalluria, urinary tract infections, hematuria, and renal failure.

Option D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is one of the major causes of severe combined immunodeficiency.

Pearl PF1567: Purine salvage deficiencies: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Adenosine deaminase deficiency(SCID)

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency(SCID):

Adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency is one of the major cause of SCID. It is also called as Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome.

SCID patients are usually affected by severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections early in life and often present with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:

It is due to deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease.

Clinical features:

* Intellectual disability

* Self-mutilation

* Aggression

* Hyperuricemia

* Gout

Treatment:

* Allopurinol

* Febuxostat
questions.learning: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase — The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement-1: In the National Immunization Program, BCG vaccine is given only on the left upper arm. Statement-2: This is done to maintain uniformity and for helping surveyors in verifying receipt of the vaccine. Which one of the following is correct?
options: Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are correct and Statement-2 is the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are correct and Statement-2 is not the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is true but Statement-2 is false.
Statement-1 is false but Statement-2 is true.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are correct and Statement-2 is the correct explanation for Statement-1.

In India’s Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), the BCG vaccine is routinely administered intradermally over the left upper arm. This standardization ensures uniformity across the country and helps health workers and surveyors verify vaccination status by looking for the characteristic BCG scar during immunization surveys.

Why?

• Statement 1. In the National Immunization Program, BCG vaccine is given only on the left upper arm✔️: True. BCG is given in the left upper arm.
• Statement 2. This is done to maintain uniformity and for helping surveyors in verifying receipt of the vaccine✔️: True. The uniform site facilitates verification of vaccination during surveys and assessments.
• Statement-2 correctly explains Statement-1. ✔️
questions.learning: Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are correct and Statement-2 is the correct explanation for Statement-1. In India’s Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), the BCG vaccine is routinely administered intradermally over the left upper arm.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with a beaded appearance of the chest on clinical examination, and the corresponding chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a "beaded appearance" on the chest, known as a rachitic rosary, combined with X-ray findings of metaphyseal fraying and cupping, is diagnostic of rickets. Rickets results from Vitamin D deficiency, which leads to impaired bone mineralization at the growth plates. Physical signs often include frontal bossing, delayed fontanel closure, and bowing of long bones. Scurvy (Option A), caused by Vitamin C deficiency, presents with a "scorbutic rosary" that is sharp rather than beaded, along with gum bleeding and subperiosteal hemorrhages. Beriberi (Option C) is due to Thiamine deficiency and presents with cardiac or neurological symptoms, while Pellagra (Option D) is due to Niacin deficiency, causing the "3 Ds" of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Treatment for rickets involves high-dose Vitamin D supplementation (Stoss therapy) and oral calcium
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a "beaded appearance" on the chest, known as a rachitic rosary, combined with X-ray findings of metaphyseal fraying and cupping, is diagnostic of rickets.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: According to the American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) classification, what grade is given to a normal healthy individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ASA I

A normal healthy individual is given ASA I grade.

Pearl PF1220: American Society of Anesthesiologists’ Physical Status Classification of Patients

American Society of Anesthesiologists’(ASA) classification is used to define relative risk prior to conscious sedation and surgical anesthesia.

It is simple, reproducible and strongly correlates to perioperative risk.

ASA PS Classification & Definition
Examples, including, but not limited to:

ASA I: A normal healthy patient
Healthy, non-smoking, no or minimal alcohol use

ASA II: A patient with mild systemic disease
Without substantive functional limitations. Eg: current smoker, social alcohol drinker, pregnancy, obesity (30 < BMI < 40), well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease

ASA III: A patient with severe systemic disease
Substantive functional limitations; One or more moderate to severe diseases. Eg: poorly controlled DM or HTN, COPD, morbid obesity (BMI ≥40), active hepatitis, alcohol dependence or abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction of ejection fraction, ESRD undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis, premature infant PCA < 60 weeks, history (>3 months) of MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents.

ASA IV: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life
Eg: recent ( < 3 months) MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents, ongoing cardiac ischemia or severe valve dysfunction, severe reduction of ejection fraction, sepsis, DIC, ARD or ESRD not undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis

ASA V: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation
Eg: ruptured abdominal/thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischemic bowel in the face of significant cardiac pathology or multiple organ/system dysfunction

ASA VI: A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Treatment of ptosis caused by Horner’s syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasanella servat operation

Fasanella servat operation is done for cases of mild ptosis (1.5-2 mm) with retained levator palpabrae superioris muscle function as seen in Horner’s syndrome.

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the loss of sympathetic supply to the muller's muscle of the lid and not due to levator muscle palsy. Fasanella servat operation is not done in patients with severe ptosis and poor levtaor function.

Option A:Levator resection is performed for moderate and severe grades of ptosis but with retained levator function. This operation is contraindicated in patients with poor levator function.

Option B: Frontalis sling also known as Brow suspension is done in patients with severe ptosis with poor or absent levator muscle function. Here, the lid is anchored to the frontalis muscle via a sling.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with difficulty breathing and cyanosis after being exposed to phosphine gas in a garage while repairing a vehicle. Despite receiving 100% oxygen, his oxygen saturation remains low and does not improve. What type of hypoxia is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histotoxic hypoxia

Phosphine causes histotoxic hypoxia by inhibiting mitochondrial function and disrupting cellular respiration at the tissue level.

Phosphine causes histotoxic hypoxia, and thus, by preventing the O2 utilization at the tissue level, it acts as a powerful stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors. Phosphine inhibits cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain. This disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, preventing ATP production despite adequate oxygen availability.

In phosphine poisoning the oxygen is present but cells cannot use it due to blocked cellular respiration. This is why simple oxygen supplementation isn't effective as a primary treatment.

Other options:

Option B: Anemic hypoxia occurs due to decreased hemoglobin in the blood capable of carrying oxygen. This can be in the form of a low amount of hemoglobin, defective hemoglobin, or interference with hemoglobin-oxygen binding. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is classified as anemic hypoxia as CO preferentially binds to hemoglobin and reduces the oxygen binding. Treatment involves terminating the exposure to CO and oxygen supplementation.

Option C: Hypoxic hypoxia refers to a reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood. It has multiple causes, like high altitude, hypoventilation, right-to-left shunts, diffusion defects, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Chronic emphysema is an example of hypoxic hypoxia, as there is alveolar destruction leading to reduced gas exchange and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. In most cases, supplemental oxygen is helpful in treatment.

Option D: Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.

questions.text: A child has elevated liver enzyme levels. A ring-like structure is noted on ocular examination as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the cause for this?

Correct answer: A. Copper

This clinical scenario of elevated liver enzymes and Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image is suggestive of Wilson's disease. KF ring is formed due to the deposition of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea.

Wilsons disease:

The autosomal-recessive disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes a membrane-bound, copper-transporting ATPase.

Clinical symptoms:

* Hepatitis and cirrhosis

* Behavioral disturbances

* Wing beating tremor

* Ophthalmic characteristics:

* Deposition of copper in the posterior capsule of the lens resulting in sunflower cataract

* KF ring

Kayser-Fleischer ring (KF) Ring:

* KF ring is a golden-brown ring formed due to the deposition of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea

* Characteristically observed in Wilson's disease but is not pathognomonic

* Does not interfere with vision

* Present in almost all patients of Wilson's disease with neurological/psychiatric symptoms

* Present only in 30–50% of patients diagnosed in the hepatic or presymptomatic state, therefore the absence of KF rings does not exclude the diagnosis of Wilson's disease

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of dilation and curettage (D&C) presents with amenorrhea. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) shows a characteristic honeycomb appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asherman syndrome involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following excessive curettage during a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure for pregnancy-related events. These adhesions obliterate the uterine cavity, leading to amenorrhea (secondary) and infertility despite normal ovulation. The diagnostic hallmark on Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is the visualization of multiple irregular filling defects, described as a "honeycomb appearance" or "shredded appearance" . Kallman syndrome (Option B) involves anosmia and low gonadotropins. Sheehan syndrome (Option C) is pituitary necrosis following postpartum hemorrhage, causing a global lack of pituitary hormones. Stein-Leventhal syndrome (Option D) is the classic name for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), which presents with irregular cycles rather than total amenorrhea following a procedure. Treatment for Asherman’s requires hysteroscopic adhesiolysis followed by hormonal therapy to regenerate the endometrium. Therefore, the procedural history and HSG finding confirm the diagnosis
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following excessive curettage during a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure for pregnancy-related events.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Reduced incidence of neural tube defects is observed with the use of ________ prior to conception.
questions.explanation: Extensive clinical research has definitively proven that the periconceptional supplementation of folic acid (Vitamin B9) significantly reduces the incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly (Option A). The recommended standard dose is 400 mcg daily for women with a low risk, started at least one month before conception and continued through the first trimester. For women with a prior history of an NTD-affected pregnancy, a higher dose of 4 mg is used. Iron (Option B) is essential for preventing maternal anemia but does not impact neural tube formation. Calcium (Option C) is vital for maternal bone health and preventing pre-eclampsia. Excess Vitamin A (Option D) can actually be teratogenic and is not used for NTD prevention. Therefore, folic acid is the only nutrient listed with a direct, preventative role in the embryological closure of the neural tube
questions.learning: Extensive clinical research has definitively proven that the periconceptional supplementation of folic acid (Vitamin B9) significantly reduces the incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly (Option A).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with weakness of the distal leg muscles and diminished deep tendon reflexes, without any sensory complaints such as tingling or numbness. Examination reveals muscle wasting below the knee. A similar clinical history is reported in his elder brother. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is a group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies. The clinical presentation of a young adult with progressive distal muscle weakness, absent reflexes, and characteristic distal atrophy ("inverted champagne bottle" legs) is classic. The fact that the patient's brother has a similar history points to a genetic etiology, most commonly autosomal dominant (CMT1A). Refsum’s disease (Option B) also features neuropathy but is accompanied by retinitis pigmentosa and ichthyosis. Neuropathy in Sjogren's syndrome (Option C) and Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) is typically acquired, not familial, and usually involves significant sensory symptoms like pain or paresthesias. CMT predominantly affects the long axons of the peripheral nerves. Patients often develop high foot arches (pes cavus) and hammertoes. Diagnosis is confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing slow velocities and genetic testing. Management is largely supportive, including orthotics and physical therapy to maintain mobility and prevent complications from foot deformities

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 13-year old boy with presents to you with limitation of abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. The X-ray appearance of his left hip joint is shown in the below image. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

The given clinical scenario and trethowan's sign seen in the x-ray are suggestive of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).

The Klein line is a line along the superior aspect of the femoral neck which normally intersects the epiphysis. In SCFE, Klein's line does not intersect the epiphysis and passes superior to it. This is known as Trethowan's sign.

Slipped femoral capital epiphysis:

SCFE occurs during the period of rapid growth with the average age of presentation around 12 years.

Risk factors: Obesity, hypothyroidism, growth hormone excess, and chronic renal failure are all-important associations of SCFE.

Clinical features:

* Patients with SCFE typically present in the rapid growth phase of adolescence with pain in the thigh, groin, or knee.

* On examination, the affected limb is shortened and externally rotated.

* There is a limitation in abduction, flexion, and internal rotation on the affected side.

* Flexion of the hip might lead to obligate external rotation and abduction - positive Drehmann’s sign.

* Patients may have an antalgic or Trendelenburg gait.

Other radiological findings include:

* Wide or irregular physis with loss of the anterior head-neck concavity

* Sharp metaphyseal border of the head

* Loss of total epiphyseal height

* Steel sign (Metaphyseal blanch sign) - The posteriorly displaced femoral epiphysis overlaps over the metaphysis causing a crescent-shaped area of increased density on the AP radiograph.

* Capener’s sign –the metaphysis displaces laterally, worsening the slip and causes a reduction in the double-density crescent created by the overlap of the posterior acetabulum and proximal metaphysis on the AP radiograph.

* Southwick angle – The angle between the line drawn perpendicular to the physis and a line parallel to the femoral shaft. As slip worsens, the Southwick angle will increase. It is measured on the frog lateral X-ray view.

Other options:

Perthes disease:

It is characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis. This condition commonly affects children of 4-8 years of age. The child has pain in the hip while performing passive movements. The radiograph shows features of bone necrosis followed by remodeling.

Developmental Dysplasia of the hip: It is characterized by spontaneous dislocation of the hip joint before, during, or shortly after birth. This condition is more common in females. Children with this condition have a waddling gait and on examination abduction and lateral rotation of the hip are decreased. X-ray shows a broken Shenton's line and the femoral head lies in the upper and outer quadrants formed by Hilgenreiner’s line and Perkin’s line.

The image given below shows the vertical Perkin's line and the horizontal Hilgenreiner's line. Normally the femoral head lies in the inner and lower quadrant formed by these lines. But in DDH the femoral head is in the upper and outer quadrant.

Ankylosing spondylitis: It is a chronic progressive inflammatory condition affecting the sacroiliac joints and the axial skeleton. It is commonly seen in young male adults and they typically present with an insidious onset back pain that improves with exercise. The earliest radiological finding is erosion and fuzziness of the sacroiliac joints and the characteristic late sign is the bamboo-spine appearance.

X-ray showing bamboo-spine appearance-

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presents with chronic diarrhoea along with a skin rash resembling acrodermatitis. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely nutritional deficiency?
questions.explanation: The combination of chronic diarrhea and a periorificial or acral rash is characteristic of zinc deficiency, often manifesting as the genetic disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica. This condition presents with a hallmark dermatitis around the mouth, hands, feet, and perineum, alongside alopecia and failure to thrive. It typically occurs due to impaired zinc absorption. Selenium deficiency (Option B) is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) but not acrodermatitis. Niacin deficiency (Option C) causes pellagra, featuring the "3 Ds" (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia), but the resulting rash is usually photosensitive and occurs in sun-exposed areas rather than periorificial sites. Magnesium deficiency (Option D) causes neuromuscular issues like tetany and seizures rather than this specific rash pattern. Zinc plays a crucial role in intestinal integrity and immune function, so its deficiency leads to both the dermatological and gastrointestinal symptoms described
questions.learning: The combination of chronic diarrhea and a periorificial or acral rash is characteristic of zinc deficiency, often manifesting as the genetic disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman presented with a BIRADS-5 breast lesion. Which of the following is a good prognostic factor for this lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ER positive

ER positivity is a good prognostic factor in breast cancer.

The ER and PR are two steroid hormone receptors present in breast cancer. The expression of these receptors indicates a favorable prognosis and response to hormonal therapy.

Other options:

Option A: The mutations in BRCA1 gene account for up to 40% of familial breast cancers. These tumors are high-grade, hormone receptor–negative, and aneuploid and do not have a good prognosis.

Option B: p53 is a tumor suppressor gene, which on mutation acts as an oncogene. p53 positivity is associated with highly malignant breast cancers and has poor survival.

Option D: Ki-67 is used to access the proliferative index (activity) of the tumor. High Ki-67 indicates a poor prognosis.
questions.learning: ER positive ER positivity is a good prognostic factor in breast cancer. The ER and PR are two steroid hormone receptors present in breast cancer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Preconceptional use of ______ leads to reduced incidence of neural tube defects.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Folic Acid

Pre-conceptional use of folic acid reduces the incidence of neural tube defects and folic acid is the commonly used active form of vitamin B9.

Folic acid deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

As per the Anemia Mukt Bharat Program, during the period of pre-conception up to the first trimester, women are advised to have 400 mcg of folic acid tablets daily to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects in the fetus.

Note that, non-pregnant, non-lactating Women of reproductive age (20–49 years) who are not actively planning a pregnancy in near term should receive 1 iron and folic acid tablet containing 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an indication to start corticosteroids in a patient with IgA vasculitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastrointestinal bleeds

The presence of gastrointestinal bleeds is an indication for corticosteroid therapy in IgA vasculitis/Henoch Schonlein Purpura.

Corticosteroids have improved outcomes in patients who develop severe GI complications including GI bleeds and intractable abdominal pain in patients with HSP. This is because it can reduce the intensity of disease and improve outcomes by helping resolve the inflammation. The other indication for the use of corticosteroids is when the patient develops crescentic glomerulonephritis, ie rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. While corticosteroids can be used for arthritis and abdominal pain, there is limited evidence of their efficacy. Thus it is strictly reserved for severe GI and renal involvement.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney resulting in vasculitis. The exact etiology of HSP remains unknown. But, it usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection caused by group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycoplasma, and Adenovirus.

Patients usually present with the following features:

• Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.
• Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.
• Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, intestinal perforation and intussusception.
• About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.
questions.learning: Gastrointestinal bleeds — The presence of gastrointestinal bleeds is an indication for corticosteroid therapy in IgA vasculitis/Henoch Schonlein Purpura.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the management of an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, which scenario is not appropriate for expectant management?
options: Initial serum beta hCG level < 1000 mIU/ mL
questions.explanation: Expectant management (observation) for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate for a highly select, stable group of patients where spontaneous resolution is likely. Standard criteria for this approach include the patient being asymptomatic (Option C), having low and decreasing serum beta-hCG levels (Option D), and an initial hCG level ideally below 1000 mIU/mL (Option A). A gestational sac size greater than 4 cm (Option B) is a definitive contraindication for expectant management and even for medical management (methotrexate). Large sac sizes carry a significantly higher risk of rupture and internal hemorrhage, necessitating surgical intervention (salpingectomy or salpingostomy). Options A, C, and D are all favorable indicators for a trial of observation. Therefore, because a large sac indicates an advanced ectopic pregnancy that is unstable, Option B is the correct "does not indicate" choice
questions.learning: Expectant management (observation) for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate for a highly select, stable group of patients where spontaneous resolution is likely.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child with short stature, skin patches, and learning difficulties presents to the outpatient department. Diagnostic workup reveals a defect in DNA repair, specifically affecting double-strand break repair. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bloom Syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by short stature, learning difficulties, and a sun-sensitive "butterfly" rash on the face (skin patches). It is caused by a mutation in the BLM gene, which encodes a DNA helicase essential for maintaining genomic stability during DNA replication and repair. While the primary defect is in DNA helicase, it manifests as a significant increase in sister chromatid exchanges and defects in repairing various DNA lesions, including double-strand breaks. Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Option B) is a defect in nucleotide excision repair, primarily causing severe photosensitivity and early skin cancers. Cockayne Syndrome (Option C) involves defective transcription-coupled DNA repair, presenting with "progeroid" (premature aging) features and microcephaly. Lynch Syndrome (Option D) is a defect in mismatch repair, primarily predisposing adults to colorectal and endometrial cancers. The combination of short stature, cognitive delay, and DNA instability specific to Bloom Syndrome makes it the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: Bloom Syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by short stature, learning difficulties, and a sun-sensitive "butterfly" rash on the face (skin patches).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following has the highest airway resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bronchi

Among the given options, bronchi (medium-sized airway) offer maximum resistance.

The best answer here is bronchi, as all the other options suggest smaller airways, while bronchi are the only medium-sized airway.

Airflow can be derived from Poiseuille-Hagen formula:

Q =π ΔPr4/8ηL

Where

• Q is the flow rate
• π is pie symbol
• ΔP is the pressure difference
• r is radius
• η is viscosity
• L is length

Also,

Flow rate (Q) = pressure difference (ΔP)/ resistance (R).

Therefore, substituting this in Poiseuille- Hagen formula,

ΔP/ R = π ΔPr4/8ηl

1/R = π r4/8ηl

R = 8ηl/ π r4

Therefore it can be derived that airway resistance is inversely proportional to the radius by the power of four.

With Poiseuille- Hagen formula we might feel that the smallest airways are the major site of resistance. However, the contribution by the smallest airways is very little to the overall total resistance. This is because, the airway branches in each generation exist in parallel rather than in series. As the parallel branching increases, the resistance decreases. (Total cross-sectional diameter of small airways put together is high). Thus the overall resistance of the small airways is very small. Also, airflow velocity decreases substantially as the effective cross-sectional area increases (i.e., the flow becomes laminar).

Other factors affecting airway resistance :

• Lung volume, as lung volume increases the resistance decreases and vice versa. Lung volume increases the transairway pressure thus increasing the caliber of the airway.
• Airway mucus, edema, and contraction of bronchial smooth muscle increase the airway resistance. Its clinical application is seen in asthma, bronchitis, and emphysema
• The density and viscosity of inspired gas also contribute to airway resistance. A gas with more density imparts more resistance.
questions.learning: Bronchi Among the given options, bronchi (medium-sized airway) offer maximum resistance. The best answer here is bronchi, as all the other options suggest smaller airways, while bronchi are the only medium-sized airway.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with history of “bones, stones and abdominal groans” due to generalized aches and pains and renal calculus colic. Which is the most discriminatory blood investigation?
options: Thyroid function tests (Free T3, Free T4, TSH)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parathyroid hormone assay

The classic presentation of “Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Overtones” is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma. The most discriminatory investigation is a serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) assay, which confirms PTH-dependent hypercalcemia.

• A. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) assay:

• Investigation of choice to confirm primary hyperparathyroidism.
• Shows elevated or inappropriately normal PTH despite hypercalcemia.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Thyroid function tests (Free T3, Free T4, TSH): Evaluate thyroid disorders and do not diagnose hyperparathyroidism.
• C. Cortisol levels: Used in adrenal disorders such as Cushing syndrome or adrenal insufficiency.
• D. Insulin and C-peptide levels: Used in the evaluation of hypoglycemia and insulinoma, not hypercalcemia.
questions.learning: Parathyroid hormone assay — The classic presentation of “Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Overtones” is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What type of cardiac murmur is depicted in the image shown below?
questions.explanation: The phonocardiogram displays a diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur occurring during systole, specifically between the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2). This pattern is the hallmark of an ejection systolic murmur. It typically begins after a short gap following S1, peaks in mid-systole, and fades before S2. This type of murmur is most commonly associated with aortic stenosis or pulmonic stenosis, where blood is forcefully ejected through a narrowed semilunar valve. A pan systolic murmur (Option B) would maintain a constant intensity throughout the entire duration of systole, commonly heard in mitral regurgitation. Diastolic murmurs (Options A and D) occur after S2 and are linked to conditions like mitral stenosis or aortic regurgitation. The visual "diamond" shape on the phonocardiogram is a definitive diagnostic feature for ejection-type pathology in medical board exams
questions.learning: The phonocardiogram displays a diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur occurring during systole, specifically between the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A child was born after 8 months of the father’s death. Grandparents filed a case that the baby might not be their son’s, but DNA came positive. What is such a child called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posthumous child

A posthumous child is one who is born after the death of the father.

• The child is conceived before the father’s death but delivered later
• Such a child is considered legitimate if paternity is established (e.g., DNA test)
• Has legal rights of inheritance from the deceased father

Why not other options:

• Suppositious child: A falsely substituted child (not biologically related)
• Fictitious child: Imaginary/non-existent
• Illegitimate child: Born outside lawful marriage (not applicable here)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Stool examination reveals a non-motile bacterium that does not ferment lactose or mannitol. Which organism is most likely responsible for his illness?
questions.explanation: The child’s presentation of bloody diarrhea (dysentery) and cramps is characteristic of a Shigella infection. The laboratory findings are the key: nonmotile, lactose non-fermenting, and mannitol non-fermenting. This specific biochemical profile identifies Shigella dysenteriae (Type 1). Shigella sonnei (Option D) is also nonmotile and lactose non-fermenting, but it is a mannitol fermenter. E. coli (Option B) is typically motile and is a classic lactose fermenter (appearing pink on MacConkey agar). Salmonella (Option C) is a lactose non-fermenter but is highly motile due to its flagella. Shigella dysenteriae produces the potent Shiga toxin, which causes extensive mucosal damage and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Because it is the only member of the Shigella group that does not ferment mannitol, the diagnosis is definitively Shigella dysenteriae. Treatment involves rehydration and appropriate antibiotics like azithromycin or ciprofloxacin
questions.learning: The child’s presentation of bloody diarrhea (dysentery) and cramps is characteristic of a Shigella infection. The laboratory findings are the key: nonmotile, lactose non-fermenting, and mannitol non-fermenting.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mlU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

This patient has an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, suggested by:

• Amenorrhea
• Abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding
• Elevated β-hCG
• Adnexal mass containing a gestational sac without cardiac activity

She is an ideal candidate for medical management with single-dose methotrexate because:

• Hemodynamically stable
• Ectopic mass <3.5–4 cm
• No fetal cardiac activity
• β-hCG relatively low (<5000 mIU/mL)

Methotrexate:

• Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
•

Stops rapidly dividing trophoblastic tissue

•

Avoids surgery

• Preserves fallopian tube and fertility

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Expectant management is reserved for falling β-hCG levels and very small ectopic pregnancies
• C. Salpingectomy is used for rupture, instability, or failed medical therapy
• D. Tubal milking has high risk of persistent trophoblastic tissue

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What could be the cause of sudden painless loss of vision?
questions.explanation: Central Serous Retinopathy (CSR) typically presents as a sudden, painless blurring of vision or the appearance of a dark spot (scotoma) in the center of the visual field. It is caused by the accumulation of subretinal fluid in the macula, often associated with stress. Chemical injuries (Option A) are extremely painful and cause immediate structural damage. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option B) and acute iridocyclitis (Option C) are both characterized by severe eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Other major causes of painless sudden vision loss include Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) and Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO). Since CSR involves a simple fluid shift without acute inflammation or mechanical destruction, it is the only painless option listed. Most cases of CSR resolve spontaneously, although monitoring is necessary to prevent permanent photoreceptor damage
questions.learning: Central Serous Retinopathy (CSR) typically presents as a sudden, painless blurring of vision or the appearance of a dark spot (scotoma) in the center of the visual field.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall on their outstretched hand. The image given below shows the cast used to manage the patient's injury. Identify the fracture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass holding position is known as the scaphoid cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion as if the glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray doesn't show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a female patient who has been recently diagnosed with mild depression, what is the recommended initial treatment approach?
questions.explanation: According to international clinical guidelines (such as NICE or APA), the "first-line treatment" for "mild depression" is psychological therapy, specifically "Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)" (Option A). CBT helps patients identify and change negative thought patterns and behaviors contributing to their low mood. Antidepressants (Options B and C) are generally "not recommended" as the primary treatment for mild depression, as their efficacy relative to placebo is much lower in mild cases than in moderate-to-severe depression. Combined therapy (Option B) is the gold standard for moderate-to-severe depression. Vagus nerve stimulation (Option D) is an invasive neuromodulation technique reserved only for treatment-resistant, severe chronic depression. For a recently diagnosed mild case, starting with non-pharmacological interventions like CBT, exercise, and sleep hygiene is the safest and most effective approach. If the patient’s condition fails to improve after an adequate trial of psychotherapy, the treatment plan should be reassessed for the potential addition of medication
questions.learning: According to international clinical guidelines (such as NICE or APA), the "first-line treatment" for "mild depression" is psychological therapy, specifically "Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)" (Option A).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with distal leg weakness, reduced muscle stretch reflexes, with no complaints of tingling or numbness. On examination, there is atrophy of the muscles below the knee. The following clinical findings are seen and similar history is seen in elder brother. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease

The given image shows lack of muscle, high arch of foot, and hammer-toes which, along with the other clinical features mentioned above, are suggestive of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy. CMT is a syndrome of many genetically distinct disorders.

CMT type 1

* Most common form of hereditary neuropathy

* Usually presents in the first to third decade of life with distal leg weakness, e.g., foot drop

* No numbness or tingling

* Reduced sensation to all modalities apparent on examination

* Reduced muscle stretch reflexes

* Atrophy of the muscles below the knee, leading to inverted champagne bottle legs

Diabetic neuropathy, primary amyloidosis, neuropathy associated with Sjogren’s syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis are acquired forms of neuropathies.

Pearl PF1592: Neuropathic Disorders

Hereditary neuropathic disorders

* Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Most common hereditary neuropathy)

* Tangier disease

* Friedreich’s ataxia

* Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy

* Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP)

* Hereditary Neuralgic Amyotrophy (HNA)

* Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy (HSAN)

* Fabry’s disease (angiokeratoma corporis diffusum)

* Refsum’s disease

Causes of acquired neuropathies

* Primary or AL amyloidosis

* Diabetic neuropathy

* Hypothyroidism

* Sjögren’s syndrome

* Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

* Scleroderma, Sarcoidosis

* Infectious (VZV,CMV,EBV,Hepatitis, HIV, Diphtheria, Leprosy)

* Inflammatory bowel disease

* Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP)
questions.learning: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease — The given image shows lack of muscle, high arch of foot, and hammer-toes which, along with the other clinical features mentioned above, are suggestive of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Inhibitors of Poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) are approved for BRCA-positive breast cancers. Which among the following drugs is used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rucaparib

Rucaparib is an inhibitor of Poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) used for BRCA-positive breast cancers.

Rucaparib is a poly ADP-ribose polymerase/ PARP inhibitor approved for the treatment of breast and advanced ovarian cancer.

PARP is a nuclear protein that transfers ADP-ribose from NAD+ to target proteins and this plays an important role in the DNA damage response. Rucaparib and olaparib are PARP inhibitors.

Inhibitors of PARP (Poly ADP Ribosyl Polymerase) approved for breast cancer:

• Olaparib
• Rucaparib
• Talazoparib

Other options:

Option A: Palbociclib is a selective inhibitor of the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6. It is used in the treatment of metastatic breast cancer.

Option C: Regorafenib is an angiogenesis inhibitor that is indicated as a second-line treatment for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma. (The first line is Sorafenib).

Option D: Vandetanib is an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor recently FDA-approved for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma.
questions.learning: Rucaparib Rucaparib is an inhibitor of Poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) used for BRCA-positive breast cancers. Rucaparib is a poly ADP-ribose polymerase/ PARP inhibitor approved for the treatment of breast and advanced ovarian cancer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the segment marked in red color in the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image shows the anatomical segmentation of the liver based on Couinaud’s classification. The red-colored area lies in the right lobe, specifically in the anterior-inferior portion. This region corresponds to Segment V, which is situated below the portal plane and anterior to the right hepatic vein. Segment V receives blood supply from the right branch of the portal vein and drains via the right hepatic vein, making it a part of the functional right liver. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option (B) IVa refers to the superior part of the left medial segment, located above the portal plane and closer to the middle hepatic vein. The red region is not in the left lobe nor in a superior position. 2. Option (C) VII represents the posterior-superior segment of the right lobe, located deep and toward the back. The highlighted region is anterior and inferior, not posterior. 3. Option (D) II is part of the left lateral superior segment, positioned high and to the left of the falciform ligament, which does not match the shown location
questions.learning: The image shows the anatomical segmentation of the liver based on Couinaud’s classification. The red-colored area lies in the right lobe, specifically in the anterior-inferior portion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is pro-apoptotic?
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is regulated by the Bcl-2 family of proteins, which act as a rheostat for cell survival. These proteins are divided into anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic members. Bax (along with Bak and Bok) is a pro-apoptotic member. It functions by promoting mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), which allows the release of cytochrome c into the cytoplasm to activate the caspase cascade. A useful mnemonic is "Bax and Bak Break" the membrane. Bcl-2 (Option A), Bcl-xL (Option B), and Mcl-1 (Option C) are all anti-apoptotic proteins. They work to preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity and prevent the release of death signals, effectively promoting cell survival. Therefore, Bax is the specific protein among the options that actively triggers the programmed cell death pathway
questions.learning: Apoptosis is regulated by the Bcl-2 family of proteins, which act as a rheostat for cell survival. These proteins are divided into anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic members.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old male with a history of chronic smoking presents with fever and a painful swelling below the left ear near the cheek region. He also has difficulty speaking or swallowing and complains of mild testicular pain. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of fever and a painful lump beneath the ear (parotitis) is characteristic of Mumps, an acute viral infection caused by a rubulavirus. The crucial clinical clue is the "mild testicular pain," which suggests orchitis, a common complication of mumps in post-pubertal males. Cervical tuberculosis (Option A) usually presents with chronic, painless "cold" lymphadenopathy. Diphtheria (Option B) is associated with a greyish-white pharyngeal membrane and severe "bull neck" swelling. Lymphoma (Option D) typically presents with painless, rubbery, and generalized lymphadenopathy rather than acute painful parotid swelling. Smoking is a distractor here, as it does not directly cause this acute constellation of symptoms. Mumps is generally a self-limiting disease, but management involves supportive care and monitoring for complications like meningitis or pancreatitis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of fever and a painful lump beneath the ear (parotitis) is characteristic of Mumps, an acute viral infection caused by a rubulavirus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The X-ray image of a child with muscle weakness and failure to thrive is attached below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickets

The clinical vignette with the above X-ray image shows fraying and cupping of the metaphysis, suggestive of rickets.

Radiological features in rickets:

* Fraying (Widening and irregularity of the growth plate)

* Cupping (Concavity of the metaphysis)

* Splaying at metaphysis (widening of metaphyseal ends)

* Generalized rarefaction

Pearl PF0381: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis.

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices.

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification (becomes denser in healing rickets, known as the white line of Frenkel).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme, which of the following is not included in the Mental Health Care Act, 2017?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Screening of family members

According to the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), screening of family members is not included in the Mental Health Care Act, 2017.

The Mental Healthcare Act of 2017 has provisions that include:

• Rights of persons with mental illness to access health care, live without discrimination and enjoy confidentiality.
• Advance directives to allow mentally ill people to make decisions about their treatment
• Procedures for admission, treatment (behavioral and interpersonal therapy, medications), and discharge
• Decriminalizing suicide and prohibiting electroconvulsive therapy unless anesthesia is used

These are achieved through the mobilization of resources to required areas, and by providing social support.
questions.learning: Screening of family members According to the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), screening of family members is not included in the Mental Health Care Act, 2017.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Good measure of systemic perfusion by ABG is by measurement of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Base deficit

Serum lactate and base deficit are the most reliable ABG-derived markers of systemic tissue perfusion. They reflect the adequacy of oxygen delivery to tissues and are widely used to assess the severity of shock, trauma, sepsis, and other states of tissue hypoperfusion.

When tissue oxygen delivery is inadequate, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, resulting in lactate production and metabolic acidosis, which is reflected as an increased base deficit.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻): Reflects metabolic acid-base status but is a less sensitive indicator of tissue perfusion than lactate or base deficit.
• B. pH: May remain normal initially because of respiratory compensation and does not specifically indicate tissue perfusion.
• D. PCO₂: Reflects ventilation, not systemic tissue perfusion.
