questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In controlled tipping, the amount of land required for the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000 is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 acre

In controlled tipping, one acre of land is required by the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000.

It is also known as a sanitary landfill. It is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal where suitable land is available. In this method, waste material is placed in a trench or other prepared area. Then, it is adequately compacted and covered with earth at the end of the day.

Methods used in controlled tipping are:

• Trench method: Done in places where level ground is available
• Ramp method: Well suited where the terrain is moderately sloping
• Area method: Used for filling land depressions, disused quarries, and clay pits
questions.learning: 1 acre In controlled tipping, one acre of land is required by the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000. It is also known as a sanitary landfill.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 72-year-old man presents with unexplained weight loss, decreased appetite, and iron- deficiency anemia. Chest X-ray shows multiple nodular opacities throughout the lungs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided chest X-ray shows numerous large, well-defined, and widely scattered round opacities in both lung fields. This is the hallmark "cannonball metastasis" pattern (Option A) . In an elderly male with weight loss and iron deficiency anemia, these nodules likely represent hematogenous spread from a primary malignancy such as renal cell carcinoma or colorectal cancer. Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option B) usually presents as a single large hilar mass. Miliary tuberculosis (Option C) is characterized by very small ( mm), diffuse "millet seed" nodules rather than large cannonball masses. Mesothelioma (Option D) causes diffuse pleural thickening rather than parenchymal balls. Therefore, because the large, discrete, and bilateral nature of the masses is pathognomonic for secondary deposits, lung metastasis is the definitive diagnosis. This radiographic finding is a classic indicator of late-stage systemic malignancy
questions.learning: The provided chest X-ray shows numerous large, well-defined, and widely scattered round opacities in both lung fields. This is the hallmark "cannonball metastasis" pattern (Option A) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which enzyme leads to the development of Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)?
questions.explanation: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) complex. This enzyme complex is responsible for the oxidative decarboxylation of the ketoacids derived from the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs): Leucine, Isoleucine, and Valine. A defect here leads to the accumulation of these BCAAs and their toxic alpha-ketoacid byproducts, which impart a characteristic sweet, maple syrup odor to the patient's urine and earwax. Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (Option B) causes Isovaleric Acidemia, which presents with a "sweaty feet" odor. Pyruvate carboxylase (Option C) and Acetyl CoA carboxylase (Option D) are involved in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis, respectively, and are not related to BCAA metabolism. MSUD is a pediatric emergency; if untreated, the leucine accumulation causes severe cerebral edema and neurological damage. Treatment involves a strict life-long diet restricted in BCAAs and specialized medical formulas
questions.learning: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) complex.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs functions as a selective α₁-adrenergic receptor antagonist in clinical use?
questions.explanation: Prazosin is a prototype selective -adrenergic receptor antagonist. By selectively blocking receptors on vascular smooth muscle, it causes vasodilation, making it useful in treating hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Phenoxybenzamine (Option A) is a non-selective, irreversible alpha antagonist that blocks both and receptors; it is primarily used in the management of pheochromocytoma. Phentolamine (Option B) is also a non-selective antagonist but is reversible and used for short-term control of hypertensive crises. Idazoxan (Option D) is a selective receptor antagonist, used more in research than in routine clinical practice. The clinical advantage of Prazosin’s selectivity for is that it does not block the receptors on presynaptic nerve terminals, thereby avoiding the massive release of norepinephrine and the resultant severe tachycardia associated with non-selective agents. Prazosin is also associated with the "first-dose effect" of orthostatic hypotension
questions.learning: Prazosin is a prototype selective -adrenergic receptor antagonist. By selectively blocking receptors on vascular smooth muscle, it causes vasodilation, making it useful in treating hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely mode of transmission of Q fever in humans?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aerosol inhalation

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted mainly from infected livestock (sheep, goats, cattle).

Primary mode of transmission:

• Inhalation of contaminated aerosols containing organisms from animal birth products, urine, feces, or milk.

Key features:

• Highly infectious organism
• Can survive in the environment as spore-like forms
• Occupational risk in farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers
questions.learning: Aerosol inhalation Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted mainly from infected livestock (sheep, goats, cattle).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following clinical features: 1. Hypomimia 2. Dysphonia 3. Festination gait 4. Cogwheel rigidity Which of the features given above are generally present in Parkinsonism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Parkinsonism is a hypokinetic movement disorder resulting from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia. It is clinically characterized by bradykinesia, along with resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability, and is associated with several characteristic motor features.

• Cardinal features: Bradykinesia (mandatory), resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and postural instability.
• Hypomimia (masked facies): Reduced facial expression due to facial bradykinesia.
• Hypophonia/Dysphonia: Soft, monotonous speech.
• Festination gait: Short, rapid, shuffling steps with difficulty stopping.
• Other features:

• Micrographia
• Stooped posture
• Reduced arm swing
• Freezing of gait
• Decreased blinking
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Parkinsonism is a hypokinetic movement disorder resulting from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with diffuse, heavily contaminated peritonitis undergoes laparotomy, after which the abdomen is intentionally left open. Which of the following measures would be most beneficial in this situation?
questions.explanation: Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is highly effective for managing an "open abdomen" in patients with severe, contaminated peritonitis. It uses negative pressure to continuously remove infected exudates and edema, reducing local inflammation and promoting granulation tissue. Normal saline-soaked gauze (Option B) only keeps the tissue moist but does not actively drain infectious material. Immediate primary closure (Option C) is strictly avoided in such cases because it carries a high risk of sepsis and abdominal compartment syndrome in a swollen, infected cavity. Antibiotic-soaked gauze (Option D) has limited benefits as it lacks the active drainage and wound contraction provided by negative pressure. VAC therapy allows for gradual wound contraction, facilitates re-entry laparotomies if needed, and eventually enables a safe definitive closure once the infection has cleared
questions.learning: Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is highly effective for managing an "open abdomen" in patients with severe, contaminated peritonitis. It uses negative pressure to continuously remove infected exudates and edema, reducing local inflammation and…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Respiratory distress syndrome is caused by the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lecithin

Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in newborns is caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, the most important component of which is lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, DPPC).

Function of lecithin (surfactant):

• Reduces alveolar surface tension
• Prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) during expiration
• Maintains lung compliance

Clinical correlation:

• Common in premature infants (immature type II pneumocytes)
• Assessed by Lecithin : Sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio in amniotic fluid

o    L/S ratio < 2 → high risk of RDS

Why other options are incorrect:

• Cephalin: Phospholipid involved in coagulation
• Sphingomyelin: Used as a reference in L/S ratio, not the main surfactant
• Cardiolipin: Found in mitochondrial membranes
questions.learning: Lecithin Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in newborns is caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, the most important component of which is lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, DPPC).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a bee sting sustained while playing outdoors. Within minutes, he develops shock, respiratory distress, and circulatory collapse. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The rapid onset (within minutes) of systemic symptoms like shock and respiratory failure following a bee sting is the classic presentation of Anaphylaxis. This is a Type I Hypersensitivity reaction, which is fundamentally IgE-mediated. Upon exposure to the bee venom antigen, IgE antibodies already bound to the surface of mast cells and basophils trigger the massive release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. This leads to widespread vasodilation and bronchoconstriction. IgG-mediated reactions (Option A) are involved in Type II and Type III hypersensitivities. IgA (Option B) is primarily an agent of mucosal immunity. T cell-mediated responses (Option D) define Type IV delayed hypersensitivity, which takes 48-72 hours to develop. The immediate life-saving treatment for an IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction is intramuscular adrenaline, which rapidly reverses the dangerous physiological changes
questions.learning: The rapid onset (within minutes) of systemic symptoms like shock and respiratory failure following a bee sting is the classic presentation of Anaphylaxis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does the neostriatum consist of?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia are organized into functional and phylogenetic groups. The "neostriatum" (or simply the striatum) consists of the caudate nucleus and the putamen. These two structures share the same embryological origin and histological appearance, characterized by medium spiny neurons that receive the majority of inputs to the basal ganglia. The "paleostriatum" refers to the globus pallidus. The putamen and globus pallidus together are anatomically referred to as the "lentiform nucleus," which is a lens-shaped mass. Thus, the neostriatum (caudate and putamen) serves as the primary "input" station, while the globus pallidus (paleostriatum) serves as the primary "output" station of the basal ganglia circuitry. Lesions or neurodegeneration in the neostriatum, such as the loss of GABAergic neurons in Huntington's disease, lead to hyperkinetic movement disorders. Accurate terminology is essential for understanding neuroanatomy and the pathophysiological basis of movement disorders commonly tested in medical examinations
questions.learning: The basal ganglia are organized into functional and phylogenetic groups. The "neostriatum" (or simply the striatum) consists of the caudate nucleus and the putamen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with a facial lesion and has a known history of acne rosacea. What is the most likely diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts rhinophyma, which is a slow-growing, benign enlargement of the nose characterized by sebaceous gland hyperplasia and fibrosis. This condition is the end-stage manifestation of phymatous acne rosacea, which explains the patient's medical history. The nose typically appears bulbous, pitted, and irregularly thickened. Rhinoscleroma (Option B) is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, presenting with "woody" hard nodules. Rhinosporidiosis (Option C) is a fungal infection (actually an aquatic protist) that causes leafy, strawberry-like vascular polyps. Scleroderma (Option D) causes the skin to become tight, shiny, and thin, which is the opposite of the thickened, pitted appearance of rhinophyma. Rhinophyma is primarily a cosmetic concern but can also lead to significant psychosocial distress and functional nasal obstruction. Treatment usually involves surgical shaving or CO2 laser resurfacing to restore the nasal contour
questions.learning: The image depicts rhinophyma, which is a slow-growing, benign enlargement of the nose characterized by sebaceous gland hyperplasia and fibrosis. This condition is the end-stage manifestation of phymatous acne rosacea, which explains the patient's medical…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo, a feeling of ear fullness and pressure, hearing loss, and a low-frequency roaring tinnitus. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic clinical tetrad described—episodic dizziness (vertigo), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness (pressure), and low-frequency tinnitus (roaring sound)—is pathognomonic for Meniere's disease. This condition is caused by endolymphatic hydrops, which is an over-accumulation of fluid in the inner ear. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) (Option B) involves brief vertigo spells triggered solely by head movement and lacks hearing loss or tinnitus. Labyrinthitis (Option C) presents with sudden, severe vertigo and hearing loss usually following a viral infection, but it is typically a single, intense event rather than intermittent episodes. Syncope (Option D) is a brief loss of consciousness due to reduced cerebral blood flow and is not associated with primary ear symptoms. Therefore, the characteristic constellation of fluctuating auditory and vestibular symptoms confirms Meniere's disease as the potential clinical diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The classic clinical tetrad described—episodic dizziness (vertigo), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness (pressure), and low-frequency tinnitus (roaring sound)—is pathognomonic for Meniere's disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Measles vaccine is classified under which type of vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Live vaccine

Measles vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine prepared from live or wild organisms grown in culture and attenuated to retain immunogenicity. It is available as a freeze-dried product and recommended only in the live attenuated form for safe and effective immunization.

The vaccine is supplied as a freeze-dried product, reconstituted with sterile diluent, and one dose of 0.5 ml contains ≥1000 viral infective units of the vaccine strain. The reconstituted vaccine is generally injected subcutaneously, but it is also effective when administered intramuscularly.

It should be stored at 2–8°C after reconstitution and used within 4 hours, since it loses about 50% potency after 1 hour at 20°C. When administered, measles vaccine induces seroconversion in 95–98% of recipients after a single dose, ensuring strong immunity.

The first dose (MCV1) is given at 9 completed months, with a second dose (MCV2) at 15–18 months to ensure full coverage.Reaching all children with 2 doses of measles containing vaccine (MCV) should be the standard for all national immunization programmes. In countries with high measles risk, MCV is also given as part of outbreak control or supplementary doses up to 5 years of age. It is often used in combination vaccines like MR (measles-rubella), MMR (measles-mumps-rubella), and MMRV (measles-mumps-rubella-varicella).

Adverse Reactions :

* After vaccination, a mild “measles-like illness” (fever and rash) may occur in 5–10 days, lasting for 1–2 days.

* Other reactions include minor upper respiratory infections, mild diarrhea, or fever that resolves in 1–3 days.

* Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) can occur if the vaccine vial is contaminated or used beyond 4 hours after reconstitution, leading to severe symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, high fever, and even death within 48 hours.

Contraindications:

* immunosuppression (e.g., HIV-infected persons with evidence of severe immunosuppression).

* Pregnancy – should be avoided for at least 4 weeks following MMR vaccination.

Persons with moderate or severe acute illness should postpone vaccination until recovery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of cholecystectomy 4 years back for gallstones presents with symptoms of obstructive jaundice. Imaging studies reveal a stone in the common bile duct. What is the most probable type of stone causing this obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Primary | Formed de novo within the bile duct itself

| Secondary | Migrated from the gallbladder into the CBD

| Retained | Missed at the time of cholecystectomy (found within 2 years of surgery)

| Recurrent | Found after 2 years of a previous stone-clear CBD

Why "Primary" is Correct Here

The key detail is the 4-year gap after cholecystectomy:

• The gallbladder has been removed → stone cannot have migrated from GB → rules out Secondary
• Discovered 4 years post-op → beyond the 2-year window → rules out Retained
• Stone formed de novo in the CBD after cholecystectomy = Primary stone

Characteristics of Primary CBD Stones

• Typically brown pigment stones (vs. cholesterol in secondary)
• Associated with bile stasis, infection (E. coli, biliary stricture)
• Often soft, earthy, and friable
• Seen with biliary stricture, periampullary diverticulum, or biliary dyskinesia
• E. coli produces β-glucuronidase → deconjugates bilirubin → pigment stone formation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: You are doing an emergency laparotomy for a case of intestinal obstruction. Which organ will you first visualize to know if this is a case of small bowel or large bowel obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Caecum

The cecum is the first organ to be visualized to differentiate between the small and large bowel in cases of intestinal obstruction.

Distension of the cecum will confirm large bowel involvement. The identification of a collapsed distal segment of the large bowel and its sequential proximal assessment will lead to the identification of the cause.
questions.learning: Caecum — The cecum is the first organ to be visualized to differentiate between the small and large bowel in cases of intestinal obstruction. Distension of the cecum will confirm large bowel involvement.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme is derived from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation: The synthesis of heme is a complex multi-step process that begins in the mitochondria. The initial, rate-limiting step involves the condensation of succinyl-CoA (from the TCA cycle) with the amino acid Glycine. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme delta-aminolevulinate synthase (ALA synthase) and requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Glutamine (Option A) is vital for purine and pyrimidine synthesis. Glutamate (Option C) serves as a neurotransmitter and a precursor for GABA and glutathione. Valine (Option D) is a branched-chain essential amino acid. Heme is the oxygen-binding prosthetic group found in hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes. Defects in the heme biosynthetic pathway lead to various types of porphyrias, which can present with neurological or cutaneous symptoms. Understanding that glycine is the fundamental amino acid precursor for heme is a core concept in biochemistry, linking protein metabolism directly to the production of essential iron-carrying molecules in the blood and tissues
questions.learning: The synthesis of heme is a complex multi-step process that begins in the mitochondria. The initial, rate-limiting step involves the condensation of succinyl-CoA (from the TCA cycle) with the amino acid Glycine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old multigravida comes to the emergency at night with an inversion of the uterus following the delivery of the baby when the nurse waited till the delivery of the placenta. Her BP is 110/70 mmHg. Pulse rate 90 beats/min. What should be the management in this case?
options: Manually remove placenta and then reposition the uterus
Reposition the uterus without removing placenta
Shift the patient to OT and reposition the uterus under anaesthesia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reposition the uterus without removing placenta

This patient with a uterine inversion with stable vitals should undergo manual reposition of the uterus without removing the placenta

Uterine inversion occurs when there is excessive traction leading to the loss of the uterine convexity and protrusion of the uterus outside the vaginal introitus.

Risk factors for uterine inversion:

• Fundal attachment of the placenta
• Uterine atony
• Attempts at cord traction before placental delivery
• Adherent placenta

There are 3 degrees of uterine inversion:

• First-degree - the fundus of the uterus inverts into the uterine cavity
• Second-degree - the uterine fundus protrudes through the cervix and lies in the vagina
• Third-degree - the whole of the uterus is inverted and protrudes through the introitus

Since uterine inversion presents with profuse bleeding and a severe degree of shock, it requires prompt diagnosis and management. It is managed by promptly repositioning the uterus by exerting a firm and constant pressure on the inverted uterine fundus. The placenta should not be removed until after the replacement of the uterus if it is still attached to the uterus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of behavioral changes over the past year, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, and poor academic performance. On examination, he has a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland. Laboratory findings show: • TSH: elevated • T4: elevated • T3: elevated Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resistance to thyroid hormone

This patient has thyroid hormone resistance (Refetoff syndrome), characterized by:

• Elevated T3 and T4 with inappropriately normal or elevated TSH
• Due to mutation in thyroid hormone receptor (TRβ) → reduced tissue responsiveness

Pathophysiology:

• Peripheral tissues are resistant → reduced negative feedback
• Pituitary continues to secrete TSH → thyroid enlargement (goiter)
• Mixed clinical picture:

• Some tissues → hyperthyroid features (e.g., hyperactivity)
• Others → relatively hypothyroid

Why not other options?

• A. Hashimoto thyroiditis → ↑ TSH, ↓ T4
• B. TBG excess → ↑ total T4 but normal TSH
• C. Dyshormonogenesis → hypothyroidism pattern

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of facial edema that has now progressed to total body swelling involving the face, abdomen, scrotum, and feet. Urinalysis revealed protein 4+ and a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 3. What is the initial treatment of choice for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prednisolone

The clinical picture and investigations are highly suggestive of minimal change nephrotic syndrome and the initial treatment of choice is corticosteroids such as prednisolone.

Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years. Its features include heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral edema. Renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) for 6 weeks followed by an alternate day dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks is recommended.

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are as follows:

* Cyclophosphamide

* Calcineurin inhibitors: Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus

* Mycophenolate

* Levamisole

* Rituximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20)

Some glomerular diseases may progress from one pattern to another or may present with considerable overlap between them, as a nephritic–nephrotic syndrome; features of nephrotic syndrome can concurrently occur with any form of nephritic syndrome but are most commonly seen with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (seen in systemic lupus erythromytosus) and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with a history of recurrent retrosternal chest pain with each episode lasting for 3-5min and subsiding with sublingual nitrate. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy and flat T-wave. He is a known case of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia currently on aspirin, atenolol, metformin, and lovastatin. What is the next best step in management?
options: Increase the dose of beta blocker
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Injection enoxaparin

The given clinical scenario of recurrent chest pain relieved on nitrates in a patient with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia are suggestive of acute coronary syndrome. ECG showing flat T wave and left ventricular hypertrophy favors the diagnosis of non-ST segment elevated acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS). Injection enoxaparin is the next best step in management.

Enoxaparin, a low molecular weight heparin, is used as a first-line anticoagulant therapy to prevent thrombosis in patients with NSTE-ACS.

Patients with acute coronary syndrome are classified into ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI) and NSTE-ACS.

Management of NSTE-ACS:

Supportive therapy - supplemental oxygen

Anti-ischemic drugs:

• Sublingual or IV nitrates
• Beta-blockers

Antithrombotic treatment consists of anticoagulants and antiplatelet therapy.

The anticoagulants used are low molecular weight heparin such as enoxaparin, fondaparinux. Other anticoagulants used are unfractionated heparin (UFH), bivalirudin, and direct oral anticoagulants such as dabigatran, apixaban, and rivaroxaban. UFH is the mainstay of therapy.

Antiplatelet drug, aspirin, is the preferred drug in NSTE-ACS treatment. P2Y12 receptor inhibitors like prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor, clopidogrel are also used. Clopidogrel is used only when prasugrel or ticagrelor are not available/ contraindicated.

GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors - eptifibatide and tirofiban - are also used as alternatives.

Invasive treatment - percutaneous coronary intervention- is done after stabilizing the patient with the above-mentioned drugs.

Other options:

Option A: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion is only given when chest pain is not relieved by sublingual nitrates. This patient has chest pain controlled by sublingual nitrates. Hence, IV GTN infusion is not recommended.

Option C: Clopidogrel is used in combination with aspirin or when aspirin is intolerable/contraindicated. However, prasugrel or ticagrelor is preferred over clopidogrel and is initiated after anticoagulant therapy.

Option D: Beta-blockers are used to reduce pain. This patient does not present with pain and also mentions that the pain is relieved on sublingual nitrates. Increasing the dose of beta-blocker has no benefit in this situation.
questions.learning: Injection enoxaparin — The given clinical scenario of recurrent chest pain relieved on nitrates in a patient with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia are suggestive of acute coronary syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the baroreceptors present in the carotid sinus?
options: They need the support of electromechanical transducers
They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer
Afferent fibres pass via cranial nerve IX
They express several non-selective cation channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer

Baroreceptors are not located in the deep smooth muscle layer. They are located in the adventitia layer.

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors which respond to stretch stimuli. They are located in the heart and adventitia of the blood vessels. There are two types of baroreceptors: high-pressure arterial baroreceptors and low-pressure volume receptors. Arterial baroreceptors are located within the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch.

The carotid sinus is a small dilation of the internal carotid artery just above the bifurcation of the common carotid into external and internal carotid branches. The afferent nerve fibres from the carotid sinus form a distinct branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), the carotid sinus nerve.

Afferent signals from both the aortic and carotid sinus baroreceptors are sent to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and they create a negative feedback loop that keeps arterial blood pressure within normal limits.

By stimulating these arterial baroreceptors in response to vascular distension, elevated arterial blood pressure can be reflexively brought back to normal levels by decreasing peripheral sympathetic outflow and activating peripheral parasympathetic outflow.

Three subsequent functional processes must take place in order to convert a mechanical change in the arterial vasculature into an excitatory signal:

1. Vascular distension and the deformation of arterial baroreceptor terminals
2. Mechanoelectrical transduction converts the mechanical deformation of arterial baroreceptor nerve terminals into baroreceptor membrane depolarization. Mechanosensitive ion channels such as the epithelial Na+ channels (ENaCs), acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) and transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels are responsible for mechanoelectrical transduction in arterial baroreceptor nerve terminals.
3. Translation of membrane depolarization into action potentials via voltage-gated ion channels (Na+, Ca2+ and K+).
questions.learning: They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer Baroreceptors are not located in the deep smooth muscle layer. They are located in the adventitia layer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Particulate matter 2.5 is an important component while calculating the AQI. If a person inhales a 2.5 particle, it gets deposited in which part of the airway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alveoli

PM2.5 particles have an aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5 µm, allowing them to bypass upper airway defences.

They penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and are deposited in the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

This deep deposition explains their strong association with cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality and their importance in AQI calculations.
questions.learning: Alveoli PM2.5 particles have an aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5 µm, allowing them to bypass upper airway defences. They penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and are deposited in the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What surgery is being performed in the image shown?
questions.explanation: The image displays the results of a total maxillectomy, characterized by the surgical removal of the entire maxilla, including its anterior, medial, posterior, and inferior walls. This procedure is typically performed for malignant tumors of the maxilla or advanced sinonasal malignancies. The wide exposure seen is achieved through a classical Weber-Ferguson incision. A total ethmoidectomy (Option A) involves removing only the ethmoid air cells for extensive sinus disease, not the maxillary bone. Partial ethmoidectomy (Option B) is even more selective, preserving healthy mucosa. A partial maxillectomy (Option D) would involve removing only a portion of the maxilla, such as the medial wall, while leaving other bony structures intact. Since multiple walls of the maxillary cavity are clearly removed in the surgical field shown, the procedure is definitively identified as a total maxillectomy
questions.learning: The image displays the results of a total maxillectomy, characterized by the surgical removal of the entire maxilla, including its anterior, medial, posterior, and inferior walls.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with chronic diarrhoea lasting four weeks. Stool microscopy reveals oval to elliptical cysts measuring approximately 16 × 20 µm. What is the most likely diagnosis
questions.explanation: Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli) is a common cause of severe, chronic malabsorptive diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. The diagnostic hallmark on stool microscopy is the presence of large, oval or elliptical, acid-fast oocysts that typically measure approximately 20–30 µm in length. Cryptosporidium (Option A) causes watery diarrhea but produces much smaller, spherical oocysts, typically 4–6 µm in diameter. Cyclospora (Option C) also presents with smaller, round oocysts (8–10 µm) that show variable acid-fast staining. Cryptococcus (Option B) is a fungal pathogen primarily associated with meningitis rather than primary chronic diarrheal illness. The specific size and elliptical shape mentioned in the clinical scenario are pathognomonic for Cystoisospora. Treatment for this infection typically involves a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) to ensure clearance and prevent recurrence
questions.learning: Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli) is a common cause of severe, chronic malabsorptive diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 80-year-old woman sustains a fall in the bathroom and presents with severe pain, inability to walk, and a shortened, externally rotated left lower limb, suggestive of a hip fracture. An X-ray confirms the injury, as shown below. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: For an 80-year-old patient with a displaced femoral neck fracture, the standard of care is hemiarthroplasty (replacing the femoral head with a prosthesis). In the elderly, femoral neck fractures have a very high risk of non-union and avascular necrosis (AVN) due to the precarious blood supply to the femoral head. Replacing the head allows for immediate weight-bearing and avoids the complications of a second surgery if internal fixation fails. Internal fixation (Option A) is preferred in "young" patients (usually years) to preserve their native joint. Meyer’s operation (Option B) is a muscle-pedicle bone graft used to treat non-union in younger patients. McMurray’s osteotomy (Option D) is an obsolete procedure for hip osteoarthritis or non-union. Therefore, in a low-demand elderly patient, the goal is rapid mobilization, which is best achieved via hemiarthroplasty
questions.learning: For an 80-year-old patient with a displaced femoral neck fracture, the standard of care is hemiarthroplasty (replacing the femoral head with a prosthesis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statistical diagram has been used in the given text to represent the change in population of a particular area between the years 1983 and 1989?
questions.explanation: The statistical diagram shown is a "Component Bar Graph," also known as a subdivided or stacked bar chart. In this representation, each bar represents the total population for a specific year (1983, 1985, 1987, 1989), and the bar is divided into segments to show the proportional contribution of different components—in this case, males and females. Option A (Histogram) is used for continuous data and features bars that touch each other. Option B (Line diagram) uses points connected by lines to illustrate trends over time. Option D (Multiple bar graphs) would place the male and female bars side-by-side for each year rather than stacking them. Component bar graphs are excellent for visualizing both the change in the total value over time and the internal composition of that total. This allows researchers to quickly identify if the gender ratio is shifting even as the overall population grows

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 10-year-old child came with complaints of pain over the right lower quadrant and lower back pain. On examination, the patient had pain over the right side of the hip on passive extension with a mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psoas abscess

The given clinical history of lower back pain, mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin and pain on passive extension of the ipsilateral hip is suggestive of a psoas abscess.

Psoas abscess is a retroperitoneal abscess, caused due to various etiologies. Previously, tuberculosis of the spine was the most common cause secondary to spreading infection from the digestive or urinary tract, which can cause psoas abscess. Nowadays, Crohn’s disease is the most common cause. Patients present with flank pain, fever and chills, malaise and weight loss. They can have referred pain to the hip, groin or knee. When the swelling extends across the groin and below the inguinal ligament along the course of the iliopsoas, it becomes cross fluctuant across the inguinal ligament.

Imaging is done by a CT scan, which shows a low-density mass with surrounding inflammation and infiltration of surrounding fat and gas or air-fluid levels.

Treatment is done by percutaneous CT-guided drainage and appropriate antibiotics.

Other options:

Option A: Pyelonephritis is usually associated with a history of urinary tract infection and sudden onset of pain in the flank and hypochondrium, not the lumbar region.

Option C: Appendicitis (retrocaecal) can present with pain on passive extension of the hip (psoas sign), but the presence of a mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin makes it an unlikely diagnosis.

Option D: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency condition presenting with sudden onset pain in the scrotum, groin and lower abdomen, tenderness, redness and edema of the scrotal skin.
questions.learning: Psoas abscess — The given clinical history of lower back pain, mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin and pain on passive extension of the ipsilateral hip is suggestive of a psoas abscess.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old child from a southern Indian state, hailing from a poor family, presents with rough and scaly skin. The child’s diet lacks vegetables and fruits. After treatment with linseed oil, Vitamin A, and Vitamin B, the symptoms subsided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phrynoderma

The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma.

Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees. They can also extend to the shoulders, neck, back, thighs, buttocks, and abdomen. It is also known as toad skin, due to the rough cone-shaped elevated papules. It can caused by deficiency of vitamins A, B complex, C, and E and essential fatty acids.

When it occurs due to vitamin A deficiency, it is associated with ophthalmic symptoms like xerophthalmia, night blindness, and Bitot's spots and cutaneous symptoms like xerosis, scaling, and acne.

Management includes nutritional improvement through diet, multivitamin supplementation, and treatment of the underlying cause.

Note: Linseed oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid, which is an essential fatty acid.

The toad skin appearance of a child with phrynoderma is given below:

Other options:

Option A: Lichen planus is a papulosquamous lesion presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules and plaques. These papules are often highlighted by white dots or lines called Wickham striae, which are created by areas of hypergranulosis. The characteristic lesions in lichen planus are shown below:

Option B: Erythroderma is a serious skin condition characterized by widespread redness (erythema) and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body's surface area. It is also known as exfoliative dermatitis and often results from underlying skin disorders, systemic diseases, or drug reactions.

Option D: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually occurs during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.
questions.learning: Phrynoderma — The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma. Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A woman in her first trimester of pregnancy is diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis and requires anticoagulation therapy. Which anticoagulant is preferred in this situation?
questions.explanation: Managing deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in pregnancy requires an anticoagulant that is effective for the mother and safe for the fetus. Enoxaparin, a Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH), is the preferred and standard anticoagulant for use throughout pregnancy. LMWHs do not cross the placenta and therefore carry no risk of fetal teratogenicity or hemorrhage. Warfarin (Option D) is strictly contraindicated in the first trimester as it is highly teratogenic, causing fetal warfarin syndrome (bone and CNS abnormalities). Betrixaban (Option C) is a Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOAC); currently, DOACs are avoided in pregnancy due to a lack of safety data and evidence that they cross the placenta. Clopidogrel (Option B) is an antiplatelet agent, not an anticoagulant, and is not used for the primary treatment of DVT. Enoxaparin provides a predictable response and generally does not require routine blood monitoring, making it the safest and most reliable choice for gestational anticoagulation
questions.learning: Managing deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in pregnancy requires an anticoagulant that is effective for the mother and safe for the fetus. Enoxaparin, a Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH), is the preferred and standard anticoagulant for use throughout pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are precipitating factors for hepatic encephalopathy? 1. Hypokalemia 2. Septicemia 3. Increased dietary protein load Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in patients with advanced liver disease or portosystemic shunting. It is most commonly precipitated by factors that increase ammonia production, decrease ammonia clearance, or worsen cerebral susceptibility to ammonia.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Hypokalemia: Correct. Hypokalemia increases renal ammonia production and promotes metabolic alkalosis, facilitating ammonia entry into the brain, thereby precipitating HE.
• Statement 2. Septicemia: Correct. Septicemia (infection) is a common precipitating factor due to increased catabolism and systemic inflammation.
• Statement 3. Increased dietary protein load: Correct. Increased dietary protein load (especially in susceptible patients) increases intestinal ammonia production and can precipitate HE.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in patients with advanced liver disease or portosystemic shunting.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tendon marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flexor carpi radialis

The tendon marked in the image is of flexor carpi radialis.

Flexor carpi radialis:

* Flexor carpi radialis arises from the medial epicondyle and its fusiform muscular belly converges in the mid-forearm into a long tendon. This tendon now passes within a synovial sheath through a lateral canal, formed by the flexor retinaculum above and a groove on the trapezium below.

* It inserts on the palmar surface of the base of the second metacarpal and sends a slip to the third metacarpal.

* Blood supply is by a branch that arises from either the anterior or the posterior ulnar recurrent artery. The distal minor pedicles supplying flexor carpi radialis are six to eight branches from the radial artery that enter the muscle on the anterolateral side.

* It is innervated by the median nerve, root value is C6, C7.

* It is a wrist flexor and acts with flexor carpi ulnaris for wrist flexion, and with the radial extensors of the wrist to abduct the hand.

* Testing is by palpating its contracting fibers during flexion of the wrist against resistance.
questions.learning: Flexor carpi radialis — The tendon marked in the image is of flexor carpi radialis. Flexor carpi radialis: * Flexor carpi radialis arises from the medial epicondyle and its fusiform muscular belly converges in the mid-forearm into a long tendon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following veins are involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to liver cirrhosis. When portal blood flow is obstructed, portosystemic anastomoses form at specific sites. At the lower end of the esophagus, the portal circulation (represented by the left gastric vein) meets the systemic circulation (represented by the esophageal veins draining into the azygos system). Increased pressure in the left gastric vein causes the submucosal esophageal veins to become dilated and tortuous, forming varices. The right gastric vein (Option B) drains the lesser curvature but is not the primary contributor to lower esophageal varices. The left gastroepiploic vein (Option C) and right gastroepiploic vein (Option D) drain the greater curvature into the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, respectively, and are not part of the esophageal portosystemic shunt. Therefore, the left gastric vein is the key portal vessel involved
questions.learning: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to liver cirrhosis. When portal blood flow is obstructed, portosystemic anastomoses form at specific sites.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.explanation: The arterial blood gas values show a pH of 7.5, indicating alkalemia. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is elevated at 33 mEq/L, which identifies the primary disturbance as metabolic. This pattern is classic in patients with recurrent vomiting, where loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) leads to a relative excess of bicarbonate in the blood. The PaCO₂ is also elevated at 48 mm Hg, reflecting appropriate respiratory compensation. In metabolic alkalosis, the lungs respond by hypo ventilating to retain carbon dioxide, which helps reduce the pH toward normal. The other options are inconsistent with these findings: 1. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) presents with low pH and low bicarbonate. 2. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) shows high PaCO₂ with a low pH. 3. Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) features high pH with low PaCO₂ due to hyperventilation. Thus, the most likely abnormality in this patient with recurrent vomiting is metabolic alkalosis, often accompanied by hypochloremia and hypokalemia due to acid and electrolyte loss
questions.learning: The arterial blood gas values show a pH of 7.5, indicating alkalemia. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is elevated at 33 mEq/L, which identifies the primary disturbance as metabolic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cancer that least commonly spreads by lymphatic route is ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Basal Cell Carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is a locally aggressive tumor that rarely spreads by the lymphatic route.

Mutations in sonic hedgehog pathway are associated with it.

It presents as small, slowly growing pearly nodule, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on its surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC).

The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

The most common site is the inner canthus of the eye.

Basal cell carcinoma does not show lymphatic or hematogenous metastasis. It is primarily locally invasive.
questions.learning: Basal Cell Carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma is a locally aggressive tumor that rarely spreads by the lymphatic route. Mutations in sonic hedgehog pathway are associated with it.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What would happen to the half-life and plasma concentration of a drug which follows first-order kinetics, if the dose is doubled?
options: Half-life doubles and plasma concentration remains the same
Half-life remains the same and plasma concentration doubles
Half-life and plasma concentration remains the same
Half life and plasma concentration doubles
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Half-life remains the same and plasma concentration doubles

In this case, the half-life remains the same, and the plasma concentration doubles.

Half-life is constant in drugs following first-order kinetics irrespective of the dose as a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time.

The plasma concentration of the drug increases when the dose given is increased. In this case, as the drug dose is doubled plasma concentration is also doubled.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exosome

Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by Exosome.

In the last decade, a class of small, heterogeneous, secreted vesicles, broadly termed as extracellular vesicles have been identified.

These extracellular vesicles have been implicated as a new and important mediator of cell-cell communication that likely contributes importantly to both normal and pathologic physiology.

These vesicles are enclosed by a lipid bilayer.

They are heterogeneous in size (30-2000 nm diameter), and are generated by at least two distinct mechanisms:

• Microvesicles are generated by budding from the plasma membrane of a source cell.
• Exosomes are generated from the multivesicular body (MVB).

Note: The terms microvesicle and exosome are often lumped together as simply exosomes.
questions.learning: Exosome Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by Exosome. In the last decade, a class of small, heterogeneous, secreted vesicles, broadly termed as extracellular vesicles have been identified.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not the treatment of amblyopia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strabismus Surgery

Amblyopia (“lazy eye”) is a developmental decrease in visual acuity due to abnormal visual experience during the critical period, and treatment aims to improve visual input and force use of the amblyopic eye.

• Amblyopia treatment aims to improve visual acuity by stimulating the weaker eye, not just correcting alignment.

Actual treatments of amblyopia:

• Occlusion therapy (patching) → gold standard
• Refractive error correction → spectacles/contact lenses
• Penalization (e.g., atropine)
• Video games / perceptual learning → newer adjunct (especially dichoptic therapy)

WhyStrabismus surgeryis NOT a treatment:

• It corrects ocular alignment (cosmesis + binocular function)
• Does NOT directly improve amblyopia
• Amblyopia must be treated before or along with surgery, not by surgery itself

First vision is fixed amblyopia), then alignment (strabismus)”.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The following image shows the retrograde ureteropyelogram of a patient with loin pain. What is the most probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydronephrosis

The given image showing dilated clubbed calyces with stricture of the left ureteropelvic junction points to a diagnosis of hydronephrosis.

Hydronephrosis refers to the dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system caused by a partial or complete blockage of urinary flow.

Investigations:

• Ultrasound is the least invasive technique for diagnosing hydronephrosis.
• Retrograde pyelography is rarely indicated but will confirm the site of obstruction before corrective surgery.
• Intravenous urogram (IVU) is helpful only if the obstructed kidney is functional. In IVU, the extrarenal pelvis is dilated and the minor calyces lose their normal cupping. In early stages, there is blunting of calyces followed by its clubbing in the late stages.
• A renal isotope scan (DTPA or MAG-3) is the best modality to confirm the obstructive dilatation of the collecting system.
questions.learning: Hydronephrosis — The given image showing dilated clubbed calyces with stricture of the left ureteropelvic junction points to a diagnosis of hydronephrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following immunodeficiency disorders is least likely to cause rejection of a mismatched transplant due to absent or severely impaired immune function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bare lymphocyte syndrome

Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome (BLS)

• There is defective expression of MHC molecules:

• Type I BLS → ↓ MHC I → affects CD8⁺ T cells
• Type II BLS → ↓ MHC II → affects CD4⁺ T cells  (more severe)

Without MHC:

• Antigens cannot be presented
• T cells cannot be activated
• Adaptive immune response collapses

Bare lymphocyte syndrome is characterized by absent MHC class II expression due to defective antigen presentation. This results in failure of CD4⁺ T-cell activation and severe impairment of cell-mediated immunity.

Transplant rejection is T-cell mediated and therefore markedly reduced in this condition.

Wiskott-Aldrich and Job syndromes retain functional T cells, while Chediak-Higashi has defective phagolysosome fusion but intact adaptive immunity.

A. Chediak–Higashi syndrome

• Defect: Lysosomal trafficking (LYST gene)
• Affects:

• Neutrophils (↓ killing)
• NK cells

• Features:

• Recurrent infections
• Albinism
• Giant granules

T-cell function relatively preserved

→ Can still mount rejection

B. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome

• Defect: WAS protein → cytoskeletal dysfunction
• Triad:

• Thrombocytopenia
• Eczema
• Recurrent infections

Combined immunodeficiency (T + B affected)

BUT:

• Not completely absent immunity

→ Still capable of some rejection

D. Job syndrome (Hyper-IgE syndrome)

• Defect: STAT3 mutation → ↓ Th17 cells
• Features:

• High IgE
• Recurrent “cold” abscesses
• Coarse facies

Problem is neutrophil recruitment, not T-cell recognition

→ Transplant rejection still possible

| Disorder | Main Defect | T-cell Function | Graft Rejection

| -------- | ----------- | --------------- | ---------------

| Chediak-Higashi | Lysosomal trafficking | Near normal | Possible

| Wiskott-Aldrich | Cytoskeleton (WAS) | Impaired | Reduced but present

| Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome | No MHC | Severely impaired | Minimal

| Job Syndrome | Th17 deficiency | Mostly intact | Possible

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presented with abdominal pain. On examination, a mass is palpated in the right lumbar region. A barium enema is done, and the image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The clinical scenario of pain abdomen with a palpable mass in the right lumbar region along with the barium enema showing claw sign is suggestive of intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a portion of the bowel is telescoped into an adjacent segment. Intussuscipiens is the one that receives and intussusceptum are the tubes that advance. The apex of the intussusceptum is more prone to ischemia which leads to gangrene.

The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic.

It can be seen in infants during the weaning period following the introduction of new food, vaccination, or upper respiratory tract infection, and the currently approved rotavirus vaccines are associated with very minimal risk of intussusception. An area of enlarged submucosal Payer's patch acts as a lead point for intussusception.

Some lead points in children are Meckel's diverticulum, intestinal polyp, inflamed appendix, submucosal hemorrhage seen in Henoch-Schonlein purpura, and intestinal duplication cysts.

Patients usually present with cramping abdominal pain, palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, vomiting, and passage of red currant jelly stools.

Diagnosis is confirmed by abdominal ultrasound which shows target sign/bull's eye sign (shown below) and pseudokidney sign (seen longitudinally).

Barium enema shows a typical claw sign (shown below). This appearance is due to the convex filling defect caused by the apex of the intussusceptum.

The image below shows the coiled spring appearance seen in intussusception. This is due to the barium in the lumen of the intussusceptum and in the intraluminal space.

Treatment of intussusception includes hydrostatic reduction by enema using contrast material or air. Surgical reduction is only done in the presence of refractory shock, suspected bowel necrosis or perforation, peritonitis, and multiple recurrences after hydrostatic reduction. An appendicectomy is an essential component of surgical management.

Option B: Sigmoid volvulus presents with abdominal pain and distension with constipation. A plain x-ray of the abdomen shows an omega sign, coffee-bean sign (shown below), or bent inner tube sign.

Option C: Duodenal atresia is commonly seen in newborns. Babies usually present with bilious/non-bilious vomiting immediately after birth. A plain X-ray abdomen reveals two foci of gas, one in the stomach and the other in the duodenum called the double bubble sign (shown below).

Option D: Intestinal obstruction presents with abdominal pain and distension with constipation. A plain x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple air-fluid levels (shown below). Normally, 3 air-fluid levels can be seen in the plain x-ray at the fundus of the stomach, at the duodenum, and at the cecum. A barium meal is usually contraindicated in acute intestinal obstruction.
questions.learning: Intussusception — The clinical scenario of pain abdomen with a palpable mass in the right lumbar region along with the barium enema showing claw sign is suggestive of intussusception.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In a mildly dehydrated child, which of the following is the recommended management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ORS and continue breastfeeding

The cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration due to acute diarrhea is oral rehydration solution (ORS) along with continued breastfeeding or age-appropriate feeding.

WHO Plan B (Some dehydration):

• Give ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours
• Reassess hydration status after 4 hours
• Replace ongoing stool losses with additional ORS
• Continue breastfeeding throughout treatment
• Add zinc supplementation for 14 days

Intravenous fluids (Ringer lactate or normal saline) are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or when the child cannot tolerate oral fluids (persistent vomiting, ileus, altered consciousness).

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal saline: Used for severe dehydration/shock, not first-line for mild or moderate dehydration.
• B. Ringer lactate: Preferred IV fluid for severe dehydration (WHO Plan C), but unnecessary if ORS can be given.
• C. Normal saline in 5% dextrose: Not recommended for initial rehydration in acute diarrheal dehydration.
questions.learning: ORS and continue breastfeeding — The cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration due to acute diarrhea is oral rehydration solution (ORS) along with continued breastfeeding or age-appropriate feeding.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 33 weeks of gestation presents for a routine antenatal visit and reports reduced fetal movements for the past two days. She has a history of gestational diabetes, with an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. To assess fetal well-being, which antepartum fetal surveillance test should be performed initially?
questions.explanation: In a patient reporting decreased fetal movements, the Non-Stress Test (NST) is the most appropriate initial screening tool for assessing fetal well-being. The NST is a quick, non-invasive method that monitors the fetal heart rate's response to its own movements. A "reactive" NST shows heart rate accelerations, indicating adequate fetal oxygenation and an intact nervous system. The Amniotic Fluid Index (Option A) assesses fluid volume but doesn't track real-time heart rate dynamics. The Biophysical Profile (Option B) is more comprehensive but time-consuming, making it a second-line test if the NST is non-reactive. The Contraction Stress Test (Option C) is more invasive and carries the risk of inducing labor, thus it is not an initial step. Therefore, given the acute concern for movement, the NST provides the fastest reliable assessment of immediate fetal status
questions.learning: In a patient reporting decreased fetal movements, the Non-Stress Test (NST) is the most appropriate initial screening tool for assessing fetal well-being.
